issue_title: Follow-ups for PR #18254 (PPTX one chunk per slide): cleanup + parity
issue_description:
## Context

PR #18254 (\`fix(go): parse PPTX one chunk per slide\`) fixes a real bug: in Go parse mode a multi-slide PPTX deck collapsed into a single chunk because \`PPTXParser.ParseWithResult\` split \`PlainText()\` on \`\f\`, which office_oxide never emits. The fix derives per-slide text from the structured IR (\`ToIRJSON\`, one section per slide) and was rewritten to reuse \`docx_ir.go\` (\`docxElementText\`), so list / nested-list / table / text-box / line-break text is no longer dropped.

The fix is correct and should merge. The items below are non-blocking follow-ups raised during review. **Contributors are welcome to open these as separate, independent PRs** — they do not all need to land together, and splitting them makes each easier to review.

## Follow-up 1 — Simplify \`buildPPTXJSONSections\` (remove the split/rejoin round-trip)

File: \`internal/parser/parser/pptx_ir.go\`

Current code flattens each slide element with \`docxElementText(el)\` and then **splits the result on \`\n\`, drops blank lines, and rejoins with \`\n\`**. This is an unnecessary round-trip: the only observable effect is that *consecutive* hard line breaks inside one paragraph collapse to a single newline.

Suggested change: append each element's text once (trimmed, and only if non-empty) as a single value, and join elements with \`\n\` — no per-element split on newlines. This removes the special "consecutive line breaks collapse to one newline" handling and the matching test assertion, making the code shorter and the intent clearer. (Whether to preserve multiple blank lines is a judgement call; the simplification is the point.)

See CodeRabbit's 2026-08-20 note on \`pptx_ir.go\` (lines ~46-50).

## Follow-up 2 — Remove Python-compat wording from comments

File: \`internal/parser/parser/pptx_parser.go\`

The doc comment on \`ParseWithResult\` still reads like a compatibility note:

> \`Mirrors the python parser.py:slides branch which forces output_format="json" for the slide family.\`

Per the repo's \`AGENTS.md\` ("do not add new compatibility wording in comments/docs"), reword to a factual description, e.g. "forces \`output_format=json\` and emits one JSON item per slide section." Comment-only; no behavior change.

## Follow-up 3 — \`doc_type_kwd: "image"\` alignment (pre-existing tech-debt)

\`ParseWithResult\` hardcodes \`doc_type_kwd: "text"\`. In the Python slide path, slides are rendered/OCR'd and carry \`doc_type_kwd: "image"\`. This discrepancy is **pre-existing** (the old \`pptx_parser.go\` also hardcoded \`"text"\`) and is out of scope for #18254. Track it separately: either emit \`doc_type_kwd: "image"\` with the base64 slide image for image-only slides, or skip empty items, so image-only decks don't produce empty \`text\` chunks.

## Follow-up 4 — Go↔Python text-format parity (bullet / table)

Even after #18254, the *text content* of a slide differs between the Go and Python parsers:

- Python \`RAGFlowPptParser.__get_bulleted_text\` (\`deepdoc/parser/ppt_parser.py\`) prefixes bullets with \`"  " * level + "."\` and transposes tables to \`header: value\` per row.
- The Go path via \`docxElementText\` emits plain text and flattens tables row-by-row (\`H1\nH2\na\nb\`).

These are pre-existing parity gaps (not introduced by #18254). This is a larger topic than the chunk-count fix and is better handled in its own PR/issue rather than widening #18254.

## Suggested split

- PR A: Follow-up 1 + 2 (small, comment/logic cleanup in \`pptx_ir.go\` / \`pptx_parser.go\`).
- PR B: Follow-up 3 (\`doc_type_kwd\` alignment).
- PR C: Follow-up 4 (text-format parity) — likely needs its own design discussion.

Each can be reviewed and merged independently.

issue_title: Bug: `<ViewTransition>` name-prop change does not trigger view transition without child DOM mutation
issue_description:
A `<ViewTransition>` whose `name` prop changes between renders does **not** trigger the view transition update pipeline unless a child DOM mutation also occurs. Hero morphs via name-prop toggling on mounted components silently produce no animation.

> **Update (2026-06-10):** A fix is now proposed in [facebook/react#36728](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/36728). The GitHub Pages live preview below has since been rebuilt against a **patched** React build that includes that fix, so it now demonstrates the *corrected* behaviour, not the bug. To see the original broken behaviour, use the CodeSandbox (unpatched canary) or check out a commit before `cf0fe598` in the reproduction repo.

## React version

- `react`: `19.3.0-canary-46103596-20260305`
- `react-dom`: `19.3.0-canary-46103596-20260305`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Mount two `<ViewTransition>` boundaries wrapping a button and a dialog
2. Toggle the `name` prop between them (one gets `"camera-hero"`, the other `undefined`) via `startTransition` + `addTransitionType`
3. No child DOM mutations occur during the transition

**Reproduction repo:** https://github.com/kjanat/react-canary-19.3.0-view-transition-bug  
**Live preview:** https://kjanat.github.io/react-canary-19.3.0-view-transition-bug/ (now serves a **patched** build that includes the fix, so it no longer reproduces the bug, see the update note above)  
**CodeSandbox:** https://codesandbox.io/p/sandbox/yx5sdy (broken version)

Toggle between **Broken** and **Workaround** modes to see the difference. Note: on the patched GitHub Pages preview both modes now animate; use the CodeSandbox above (unpatched canary) to observe the original broken vs. workaround contrast.

Minimal repro component:

```tsx
<ViewTransition
  name={heroOwner === 'button' ? 'camera-hero' : undefined}
  share="camera-hero-morph"
  default="none"
>
  <button>Use live camera</button>
</ViewTransition>

<ViewTransition
  name={heroOwner === 'dialog' ? 'camera-hero' : undefined}
  share="camera-hero-morph"
  default="none"
>
  <dialog ref={dialogRef}>{modalContent}</dialog>
</ViewTransition>
```

The `heroOwner` state toggles between `'button'` and `'dialog'` inside `startTransition` with `addTransitionType('camera-modal')`.

## Expected behavior

Opening the modal morphs smoothly from the trigger button to the dialog (shared `camera-hero` element with CSS view-transition animations).

## Actual behavior

Modal appears instantly -- no hero morph animation. See [root cause §1](#1-name-only-changes-do-not-produce-update) for the code path that leads to a zero-opacity cancellation.

### Workaround

Two changes required simultaneously (visible in workaround mode in the reproduction):

1. **`update` prop** -- unblocks VT processing (otherwise `default='none'` gates it out):
   ```tsx
   update={{ default: 'none', 'camera-modal': 'camera-hero-morph' }}
   ```
2. **Forced child DOM mutation** -- sets the internal `Update` flag on the VT fiber:
   ```tsx
   <button data-hero-owner={heroOwner}>Use live camera</button>
   ```

The `data-hero-owner` attribute serves no purpose other than forcing a child DOM mutation that sets a flag which logically should depend on the name change itself.

## Root cause (source references)

All references below are GitHub permalinks to React commit [`4610359651fa10247159e2050f8ec222cb7faa91`][react-commit], matching `react-dom@19.3.0-canary-46103596-20260305`.

### 1. Name-only changes do not produce `Update`

In [`measureViewTransitionHostInstancesRecursive`][measure-recursive], the `Update` flag gates whether `applyViewTransitionName` fires for the new snapshot:

```js
(parentViewTransition.flags & Update) !== NoFlags
  && applyViewTransitionName(instance, newName, className);
```

In this code path, the `Update` flag is set in the mutation phase ([`ReactFiberCommitWork.js#L2634-L2645`][update-flag-set]) when `viewTransitionMutationContext` is `true`:

```js
viewTransitionMutationContext && (finishedWork.flags |= Update);
```

`viewTransitionMutationContext` becomes `true` when a DOM mutation (attribute change, text change, element insertion/removal) occurs within the VT's child subtree during the mutation commit. The `Update` flag can also be set during measurement if `hasInstanceChanged()` detects a bounding-rect change ([L676-681][has-instance-changed]), but in this scenario (name-only prop change, no layout shift), measurements are identical and this path returns false.

When only the VT's `name` prop changes, with no child mutations and no layout change, the flag stays `NoFlags`. Without `Update`, the instance is not passed to `applyViewTransitionName` but is instead pushed to `viewTransitionCancelableChildren`, which leads to a zero-opacity cancellation path in [`ReactFiberConfigDOM.js#L1616-L1640`][cancel-animation]:

```js
current.animate(
  { opacity: [0, 0], pointerEvents: ['none', 'none'] },
  { duration: 0, fill: 'forwards', pseudoElement: '::view-transition-group(' + oldName + ')' },
);
```

> **Note:** this cancellation path is only reachable when the `update` prop unblocks before-mutation snapshot capture and after-mutation measurement. With `default='none'` and no `update` prop, host instances never receive VT names in the first place, so they never reach `viewTransitionCancelableChildren`. The zero-opacity cancellation manifests specifically in the partial-workaround state (setting `update` without also forcing a DOM mutation).

React already detects the name change in `beginWork` at [`ReactFiberBeginWork.js#L3617-L3622`][name-change-detected]:

```js
if (current !== null && current.memoizedProps.name !== pendingProps.name) {
  workInProgress.flags |= Ref | RefStatic;
}
```

This sets `Ref | RefStatic` for ref lifecycle, but it does not propagate into the commit phase as a VT update signal.

### 2. `default='none'` gates out the update path (compounding)

The `share` prop name suggests it controls shared-element/hero morphs, but in the source it is consulted in the **enter/exit pair** path ([`commitEnterViewTransitions`][commit-enter] and [`commitExitViewTransitions`][commit-exit]) and not in the update path. When both VTs stay mounted and only change their `name` prop, React routes through the **update** path, which calls `getViewTransitionClassName(props.default, props.update)` in two phases:

| Phase           | Source permalink                                                       | Gate                                                                |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Before-mutation | [`ReactFiberCommitViewTransitions.js#L489-L513`][before-mutation-gate] | Class name `=== 'none'` → skip old-snapshot VT name application     |
| After-mutation  | [`ReactFiberCommitViewTransitions.js#L768-L803`][after-mutation-gate]  | Class name `=== 'none'` → skip measurement and new-snapshot VT name |

The mutation phase ([`ReactFiberCommitWork.js#L2623-L2633`][update-mutation-gate]) also checks the class name to set `inUpdateViewTransition`, but this variable controls Portal context propagation in the traced code path -- the `Update` flag assignment at [L2634-L2645][update-flag-set] is gated by `viewTransitionMutationContext`, not by the class name.\
So `default='none'` blocks the before/after-mutation phases, while the missing DOM mutation independently blocks the `Update` flag.

### 3. Separate observation: `share` not consulted in update path

The `share` prop is only consulted in the enter/exit pair path and not in the update path. This may be by-design (the update path handles DOM mutations, not shared-element pairing), but the documentation is silent on the expected behavior when only `name` changes on a mounted `<ViewTransition>`.

## Suggested fix

The name-change detection in [`beginWork`][name-change-detected] (`current.memoizedProps.name !== pendingProps.name`) could additionally set the `Update` flag or an equivalent signal, so the commit phase treats the VT as updated even without child DOM mutations.

A cleaner alternative is to keep the fix local to the mutation-phase commit handler for `ViewTransitionComponent`, adding a name-change check alongside `viewTransitionMutationContext`:

```js
} else if (
  viewTransitionMutationContext
  || current.memoizedProps.name !== finishedWork.memoizedProps.name
) {
  finishedWork.flags |= Update;
}
```

This would keep the `Update` flag closer to its apparent current usage (set during mutation phase, consumed in measurement) without changing `beginWork` flag behavior.

Additionally, the `share` className may need to be consulted in the update path when a name change is detected, not only in the enter/exit pair path.

## Docs note

The `<ViewTransition>` documentation distinguishes `share` (enter/exit pairing) from `update` (DOM mutations / layout effects), but does not clarify what should happen when only the `name` prop changes across already-mounted `<ViewTransition>` boundaries. It's unclear whether mounted name toggling is expected to produce a transition or is intentionally unsupported.

issue_title: Bug: false "change in the order of Hooks" warning when a component suspends twice via use()
issue_description:
## Summary A component that suspends **twice** in one mount via two `use()` calls on two different pending promises ends up with a corrupted `_debugHookTypes`, and the next ordinary render logs > React has detected a change in the order of Hooks called by X. This will lead to bugs and errors if not fixed. The component does not break any rule of hooks. The real hook chain is fine — only the DEV hook-type record is wrong. The trigger requires the hooks between the two `use()` calls to all be **non-stateful** (`useContext`, `useDebugValue`), because those do not advance the work-in-progress hook cursor. ## React version `react` / `react-dom` 19.2.8. The relevant code appears unchanged on `main`. ## Steps to reproduce Dev build, no framework: ```jsx import React, { createContext, useContext, useState, useEffect, use, Suspense } from "react"; import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client"; // Settled before the first render, but not yet tracked by React, // so each use() suspends once and React replays the component. const userPromise = Promise.resolve("user"); const companyPromise = Promise.resolve("company"); const A = createContext("a"); const B = createContext("b"); const C = createContext("c"); const D = createContext("d"); const E = createContext("e"); function Page() { useContext(A); useContext(B); useContext(C); use(userPromise); // first suspend useContext(D); // <-- gets recorded twice use(companyPromise); // second suspend useContext(E); const [n, setN] = useState(0); useEffect(() => { setN(1); }, []); // forces one update render return
rendered {n}
; } createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render( loading}> ); ``` ## Expected No warning. `Page` calls the same hooks in the same order on every render. ## Actual ``` React has detected a change in the order of Hooks called by Page. ... Previous render Next render ------------------------------------------------------ 1. useContext useContext 2. useContext useContext 3. useContext useContext 4. useContext useContext 5. useContext useContext 6. useContext useState ``` `Page` has five `useContext` calls, but the recorded list holds six. ## What happens Traced by logging from `mountHookTypesDev` / `updateHookTypesDev` / `renderWithHooks` / `finishRenderingHooks`: 1. **Mount attempt.** `HooksDispatcherOnMountInDEV` pushes `A, B, C`, then `use(userPromise)` throws. `hookTypesDev` has 3 entries. 2. **Replay.** `renderWithHooksAgain` resets `hookTypesUpdateIndexDev` to `-1` but leaves `hookTypesDev` as it is, and installs the rerender dispatcher. `A, B, C` verify. `use(userPromise)` resolves, and `useThenable` switches the dispatcher back to `HooksDispatcherOnMountInDEV` because the work-in-progress hook cursor has no next hook. `D` is then **pushed** (4 entries). `use(companyPromise)` throws. 3. **Second replay.** `A, B, C` verify again. `use(userPromise)` resolves; the cursor is *still* empty, because `useContext` is not a stateful hook and never advanced it — so `useThenable` switches to the mount dispatcher again and `D` is **pushed a second time** (5 entries). The rest of the component then mounts on top. 4. The committed `_debugHookTypes` is one entry too long. The next ordinary render compares its real hooks against it and warns at the first `useState`. The root cause is that `mountHookTypesDev` appends to `hookTypesDev` without truncating it to `hookTypesUpdateIndexDev + 1` — the number of entries actually re-verified in this pass. On a single suspend the leftover happens to end exactly where the mount resumes, so nothing is duplicated and the bug is invisible. ## Variants | shape | warns | | --- | --- | | two `use()`, different pending promises, `useContext` between | **yes** | | a single `use()` | no | | two `use()` on the same promise | no | | two `use()` with a `useState` between them | no | | two `use()` back to back, nothing between | no | The `useState` row is the tell: a stateful hook advances the cursor, so `useThenable` does not switch dispatchers and nothing is re-pushed. ## Why it matters `_debugHookTypes` only feeds this warning and DevTools' hook inspection, so there is no runtime impact. But the warning tells people their code "will lead to bugs and errors", and the natural response is to go looking for a rules-of-hooks violation that is not there. It also degrades the real diagnostic: `warnOnHookMismatchInDev` is guarded by `didWarnAboutMismatchedHooksForComponent`, which fires **once per component name**. A false positive consumes that component's only warning, so a genuine hook-order violation in the same component afterwards is silent. This shape is easy to hit in application code — any two data hooks that each read a context and then `use()` their own promise, called one after the other. Related report against a data library: https://github.com/vercel/swr/issues/2849

issue_title: [Feature Request] Merge XTCP and STCP — add mode: stcp-only / xtcp-only / xtcp-first
issue_description:
### Describe the feature request

## Feature Description

Unify XTCP (P2P direct) and STCP (server relay) into a single proxy/visitor type, with a configurable `mode` option that controls the transport strategy. This would eliminate the need to define two separate proxies and visitors just to get P2P with fallback.

## Motivation

XTCP and STCP are **functionally identical** from the user's perspective — both expose a private service behind a secret key. The only difference is the transport layer:

| Feature | STCP | XTCP |
|---------|------|------|
| Data path | visitor → frps → proxy (relayed) | visitor ↔ proxy (direct P2P) |
| NAT compatibility | Any (as long as frps is reachable) | Limited (symmetric/CGNAT may block) |
| Server bandwidth cost | High (all data flows through server) | None (only signaling) |
| Performance | Limited by server uplink | Limited by P2P link |

Today, if a user wants "XTCP first, fallback to STCP", they must:

1. Define a `[[proxies]]` with `type = "stcp"` on the server side — **and** a separate `[[proxies]]` with `type = "xtcp"` (with the same secretKey, localIP, localPort).
2. Define a `[[visitors]]` with `type = "xtcp"` on the visitor side, with `fallbackTo = "some_stcp_visitor_name"` pointing to a second `[[visitors]]` with `type = "stcp"`.

This is cumbersome, error-prone, and requires users to understand the internal architecture. The README even says:

> "Note that it may not work with all types of NAT devices. You might want to fallback to stcp if xtcp doesn't work."

But the current `fallbackTo` mechanism only transfers to another visitor — it doesn't auto-create the paired STCP setup.

## Proposed Solution

Introduce a new unified type `type = "stcp"` (keeping backward compatibility) with a `mode` option on both proxy and visitor sides.

### Proxy side (exposing the service)

```toml
[[proxies]]
name = "secret_ssh"
type = "stcp"
mode = "xtcp-first"          # new field: "stcp-only" | "xtcp-only" | "xtcp-first"
secretKey = "abcdefg"
localIP = "127.0.0.1"
localPort = 22
```

When `mode = "xtcp-first"`, the proxy registers itself both as a STCP proxy (visitor listener for relay connections) AND as an XTCP proxy (NatHoleController for P2P signaling). The visitor decides the actual transport.

### Visitor side (accessing the service)

```toml
[[visitors]]
name = "secret_ssh_visitor"
type = "stcp"
mode = "xtcp-first"          # same modes
serverName = "secret_ssh"
secretKey = "abcdefg"
bindAddr = "127.0.0.1"
bindPort = 6000
# Optional: P2P timeout before falling back to STCP relay
fallbackTimeoutMs = 1000     # already exists in XTCP visitor config
```

### Behavior by mode

| Mode | Proxy behavior | Visitor behavior |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| `stcp-only` (default) | Register as STCP only (current STCP behavior) | Connect via server relay (current STCP behavior) |
| `xtcp-only` | Register as XTCP only (current XTcp behavior) | Attempt P2P NAT hole punch; fail if unsuccessful (current XTCP behavior without fallback) |
| `xtcp-first` | Register as both STCP + XTCP | Attempt P2P NAT hole punch first; if not established within `fallbackTimeoutMs`, automatically dial a server-relayed visitor connection (transparent fallback, no separate visitor config needed) |

### Key Design Points

1. **Single configuration** — One proxy block and one visitor block handle both transports. No need to define paired stcp/xtcp blocks.
2. **Transparent fallback** — In `xtcp-first` mode, the visitor internally implements the fallback logic without requiring a second `[[visitors]]` entry. If the NAT hole punch succeeds, subsequent connections reuse the P2P tunnel. If it fails, the connection is relayed through frps.
3. **Backward compatible** — `type = "stcp"` without `mode` defaults to `stcp-only` (unchanged behavior). `type = "xtcp"` without `mode` defaults to `xtcp-only` (unchanged behavior). Existing configs continue to work.
4. **Implementation reuse** — The existing `XTCPVisitor.fallbackTo + TransferConn` mechanism can serve as a starting point. Instead of transferring to another explicitly-declared visitor, the XTCP visitor would internally dial a server-relayed connection via the same `dialRawVisitorConn` + `wrapVisitorConn` path used by STCP.

## Implementation Sketch

### Server side (`server/proxy/`)
- When `mode = "xtcp-first"`, the proxy calls both `startVisitorListener(...)` (STCP) and `NatHoleController.ListenClient(...)` (XTCP).
- This is essentially a composite proxy that delegates to both internal handlers.

### Client visitor side (`client/visitor/`)
- A new `UnifiedSTCPVisitor` (or enhanced `XTCPVisitor`) that:
  1. If mode is `stcp-only`: behaves exactly as the current `STCPVisitor`.
  2. If mode is `xtcp-only`: behaves exactly as the current `XTCPVisitor` (without `fallbackTo`).
  3. If mode is `xtcp-first`:
     - First tries to open a P2P tunnel (current XTCP `openTunnel` logic).
     - If the P2P tunnel isn't ready within `fallbackTimeoutMs`, falls back to `dialRawVisitorConn` + `wrapVisitorConn` (current STCP path).
     - Once P2P is established, subsequent connections use the P2P tunnel.
     - If P2P tunnel drops (e.g., NAT rebinding), new connections transparently fall back to relay while a new hole is punched.

## Alternatives Considered

1. **Status quo (manual dual config + fallbackTo)** — Already exists but requires too much boilerplate. Users shouldn't need to understand frp internals to get reliable P2P-with-fallback.
2. **A separate `[[fallback]]` section** — Would be just as verbose and harder to read.
3. **New type name (e.g., `"p2p"`)** — Would break backward compatibility and confuse users. Reusing `"stcp"` with a mode field is cleaner.

## Related

- The existing `fallbackTo` / `fallbackTimeoutMs` fields on `XTCPVisitorConfig`
- The existing `XTCPProxyConfig` and `STCPProxyConfig` (which already share the same fields: `Secretkey`, `AllowUsers`)
- README section "P2P Mode" already warns users to fall back to STCP if XTCP doesn't work

issue_title: ponytail-audit: no pass to flag AI-shaped test brittleness (fixture-name branches in prod, snapshot/mock-only assertions, 1:1 method-mirror tests)
issue_description:
ponytail's test stance is minimal and construction-time: "non-trivial logic leaves one runnable check." But `ponytail-audit`, scanning existing code, has no pass to flag AI-generated *test* slop, which is a distinct and common failure mode:

- tests that mirror implementation methods 1:1 (break on any refactor; they assert structure, not behavior)
- snapshot-only or mock-call-only assertions (they pin the AI's own output, not observable behavior)
- worst: fixture-name / id / timestamp branches leaking into *production* code to make a test pass

These pass CI and expose no deletable abstraction, so the ladder skips them, but they're maintainability slop, and the fixture-branch-in-prod case is also a correctness smell (production behavior special-cased for test data).

Distinct from #602, which is about ponytail constraining the agent *while writing* tests; this is the *audit* skill *detecting* brittleness in tests that already exist.

Suggested: one `## Hunt` bullet: fixture-name/id/timestamp branches in production code (encode the real invariant instead); snapshot-only / mock-call-only assertions (prefer observable behavior); tests that mirror methods 1:1 rather than behaviors.

Source: Google Testing Blog, "Test Behaviors, Not Methods."

issue_title: Loader.validateOptions() is only called by the GUI import dialogs - on purpose?
issue_description:
`Loader.validateOptions(ByteProvider, LoadSpec, List<Option>, Program)` reads as the place a loader validates its options, and a loader author will naturally put "this option value is unusable" checks there. As of 12.1.3 it is invoked from exactly three places, all interactive dialogs:

* `ghidra/plugin/importer/ImporterDialog.java:442` 
* `ghidra/plugin/importer/AddToProgramDialog.java:82`
* `ghidra/plugin/importer/LoadLibrariesOptionsDialog.java:60`

It is not called by `ProgramLoader`, by `HeadlessAnalyzer`/`analyzeHeadless`, by `GhidraScript.importFile`/`importFileAsBinary`, or by the GUI's own batch importer (`ImportBatchTask`). So option validation runs for a single-file GUI import and nowhere else: a headless import, a script import or a batch import with an invalid option value goes straight to `load()` with whatever the option holds.

Git logs show this behavior dates back at least as far as the original open-source commit. Whether "GUI-only" was intended is not recorded anywhere I could find; the javadoc says only "Validates the Loader's options and returns null if all options are valid", which reads as a general contract.

A loader that relies on `validateOptions()` as a safety gate is silently unprotected on every non-interactive path, and those are the paths CI, scripting and bulk imports use. In my own extension I only noticed because a headless regression fixture passed an option value the dialog would have rejected. The workaround is straightforward: treat `load()` as the authoritative validation point and factor the check into a helper both methods call.  But nothing in the API tells a loader author they need to.

Either of two outcomes would resolve this:

1. **Document it.** A sentence on `Loader.validateOptions()`'s javadoc stating that it is invoked only by the interactive import dialogs, and that `load()` must enforce anything that must hold headlessly. Smallest change, no behaviour change.
2. **Wire it up.** Have `ProgramLoader` call `validateOptions()` before `load()` and fail the import on a non-null result, so the contract holds everywhere. This is the more useful outcome but changes headless behavior for any loader whose `validateOptions()` is stricter than its `load()`.  Probably rare, but it is a behavior change and I would understand preferring option 1.

I'm happy to submit a PR for whichever you prefer.

issue_title: runtime: allocation profile is stale when collected multiple times before GC happens
issue_description:
### Go version

go version go1.27.1 darwin/arm64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
N/A
```

### What did you do?

Ran this program:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
	"runtime/debug"
)

func sampledAllocs() int64 {
	n, _ := runtime.MemProfile(nil, true)
	var p []runtime.MemProfileRecord
	for {
		p = make([]runtime.MemProfileRecord, n+50)
		var ok bool
		n, ok = runtime.MemProfile(p, true)
		if ok {
			break
		}
	}
	var allocs int64
	for _, r := range p[:n] {
		allocs += r.AllocBytes
	}
	return allocs
}

func main() {
	debug.SetGCPercent(-1)
	runtime.MemProfileRate = 1
	var b [][]byte
	for range 4 {
		b = append(b, make([]byte, 1<<20))
		var stats runtime.MemStats
		runtime.ReadMemStats(&stats)
		fmt.Println(sampledAllocs(), stats.HeapAlloc)
	}
	runtime.KeepAlive(b)
}

```

### What did you see happen?

The number of bytes allocated, estimated by the profiler, is the same every time:

```
% go run .
1050720 1232328
1050720 2298976
1050720 3366096
1050720 4433120
```

### What did you expect to see?

I expected the value to update as the program did more allocation. Something closer to:

```
% go run .
1067104 1252832
2135800 2319480
3202920 3386600
4269944 4453624
```

From the `runtime/pprof` [docs](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/pprof#hdr-Heap_profile-Profile): "If there has been no garbage collection at all, the heap profile reports all known allocations."

---

In `memProfileInternal` we'll accumulate memory profile data into the "active" records early if we don't see any non-zero values, under the assumption that GC hasn't happened yet: https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.27.1/src/runtime/mprof.go#L964-L982. But after that, we'll see non-zero values in the active records. That means we won't accumulate again, even if GC still hasn't happened.

Fixing this seems a little tricky. The memory profiler has a multi-cycle accumulation strategy, intended to give a consistent heap snapshot and avoid biasing towards allocs, where an allocation won't be counted in the "active" record until two mark terminations after when it was sampled. Maybe the right approach is to do early accumulation until we've seen two mark terminations (e.g. until `mProf_NextCycle` is called twice) following the first sample? After that point I think we'd want to stop doing early accumulation and follow the normal multi-cycle accumulation scheme.

Of course, if someone isn't trying to completely avoid doing GC, they can just call `runtime.GC()` and get an up-to-date profile.

issue_title: Related content: Partial-text indexing
issue_description:
When specifying the indices for related content, it would be useful to specify that some of them were split by word, so that their text could be matched partially. This would allow the title to be used for more in-depth indexing, rather than requiring the user to specify tags / keywords.

This would likely increase memory usage and decrease performance, so should definitely be opt-in!

I suspect common words (a, an, the etc) might want to be ignored? Although doing that in a sane, i18n-friendly manner might be a challenge!

issue_title: 更正：MaxMetaspaceSize如果不指定大小的话，不会耗尽内存
issue_description:
#### 问题截图：

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/35131874/119233517-278efe00-bb5c-11eb-9e53-31d4afe8dd56.png)

#### 关于元空间：

使用Java 8以后，关于元空间的JVM参数有两个：`-XX:MetaspaceSize=N`和 `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=N`，对于64位JVM来说，元空间的默认初始大小是20.75MB，默认的元空间的最大值是无限。MaxMetaspaceSize用于设置metaspace区域的最大值，这个值可以通过mxbean中的MemoryPoolBean获取到，如果这个参数没有设置，那么就是通过mxbean拿到的最大值是-1，表示无穷大。

由于调整元空间的大小需要Full GC，这是非常昂贵的操作，如果应用在启动的时候发生大量Full GC，通常都是由于永久代或元空间发生了大小调整，基于这种情况，一般建议在JVM参数中将MetaspaceSize和MaxMetaspaceSize设置成一样的值，并设置得比初始值要大。

#### 源码分析

MetaspaceSize表示metaspace首次使用不够而触发Full GC的阈值，只对触发起作用，原因是：垃圾搜集器内部是根据变量 `_capacity_until_GC`来判断metaspace区域是否达到阈值的，初始化代码如下所示：

```javascript
void MetaspaceGC::initialize() {	
  // Set the high-water mark to MaxMetapaceSize during VM initializaton since	
  // we can't do a GC during initialization.	
  _capacity_until_GC = MaxMetaspaceSize;	
}
```

GC收集器会在发生对metaspace的回收会，会计算新的capacityuntil_GC值，以后发生FGC就跟MetaspaceSize没有关系了。

#### 关于MetaspaceSize默认值

MetaspaceSize的默认大小取决于平台，范围从12 MB到大约20 MB，具体参考官方说明文档。

官方文档地址：

```java
https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/vm/gctuning/considerations.html
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/35131874/119233895-9fa9f380-bb5d-11eb-801c-94667fa7075a.png)

##### 那么默认不设置的时候就如下所示：

```java
-XX:MetaspaceSize=12M/20M
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=N
```

### 那么问题来了,此时MaxMetaspaceSize会耗尽内存吗?

继续查看那篇官方文，具体查看截图所示：

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/35131874/119234320-e8fb4280-bb5f-11eb-9091-d98572eff0e8.png)

##### 翻译后如下：

卸载相应的Java类时，将重新分配类元数据。 Java类是作为垃圾回收的结果而卸载的，并且可以引发垃圾回收以便卸载类和取消分配类元数据。当用于类元数据的空间达到一定级别（高水位线）时，将引发垃圾回收。垃圾收集之后，高水位线可能会升高或降低，具体取决于类元数据释放的空间量。高水位线将被抬高，以免过早引起另一次垃圾收集。高水位线最初设置为命令行选项MetaspaceSize的值。根据选项MaxMetaspaceFreeRatio和MinMetaspaceFreeRatio来升高或降低它。如果可用于类元数据的承诺空间占类元数据的总承诺空间的百分比大于MaxMetaspaceFreeRatio，则高水位线将降低。如果小于MinMetaspaceFreeRatio，则高水位线将升高。



#### 注意MaxMetaspaceFreeRatio

将元空间限制从其有效的无限默认值减少将具有完全不同的目的：避免无限的元空间增长。

**问题是那只是一个上限。实际提交的（即_当前元_空间的大小）将较小。实际上，有一个名为`MaxMetaspaceFreeRatio`（默认为70％）的设置，这意味着实际的元空间大小永远不会超过其占用率的230％。**

而要使其增长，首先必须将其填满，强制进行垃圾回收（元空间已满），以尝试释放对象，并且只有当它不能满足其`MinMetaspaceFreeRatio`（默认40％）目标时，才将_当前元_ 空间扩展到不超过GC周期后占用率达到230％。

因此，在实践中，除非应用程序不断泄漏类装入器/类或生成大量动态代码，否则实际的元空间大小应稳定在与其实际需要接近的范围内。

#### JDK默认有设置MaxMetaspaceSize的值，和服务器配置有关

不过就算有以上的要求，以上还是有风险导致本地内存无限增长，但是使用如下命令查看本机参数后：

```java
java -XX:+PrintFlagsInitial
```

会发现防止因为某些情况导致Metaspace无限的使用本地内存，影响到其他程序。在本机上该MaxMetaspaceSize参数有默认值，本人window上默认值为4294967295B（大约4096MB），在Linux下为同样可以查询其默认值。

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/35131874/119234937-b99a0500-bb62-11eb-96dd-41f038bebf76.png)

#### 结论：

**MaxMetaspaceSize如果不指定大小的话，不会耗尽内存**，原因如下：

1. MetaspaceSize的扩容会Full GC， 回收后程序有更多可用空间，可能之后空间够用不会再触发扩容。
2. MaxMetaspaceFreeRatio控制高水位，要使其增长，首先必须将其填满，强制进行垃圾回收（元空间已满），以尝试释放对象，并且只有当它不能满足其`MinMetaspaceFreeRatio`（默认40％）目标时，才将当前元 空间扩展到不超过GC周期后占用率达到230％，垃圾收集之后，高水位线可能会升高或降低。
3. -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=N 这个参数用于限制Metaspace增长的上限，防止因为某些情况导致Metaspace无限的使用本地内存，影响到其他程序。在本机上该参数的默认值为4294967295B（大约4096MB）。

issue_title: Deduplicate resources published to /public
issue_description:
I think I have thought about this before, but here it is again.

The way Hugo bundles resources (images etc.) creates potentially lots of duplication in `/public` (the same file published in different folders).

The thing is, I don't care too much about how these URLs look, but I do care about transfer speeds and disk space on my web server. I do understand that others may not share this ideal, so this will most likely be optional ...

One way of doing this would probably to create some symlinks, but that is not very portable (Apache supports it), and also probably not a great idea from a security standpoint.

issue_title: Ghidra crashes with a fatal JVM SIGSEGV when a Python script is executed after a Torch-based Python script has previously been run in the same session
issue_description:
Ghidra Crash When Re-running Python Script in Same Session

### Describe the bug

Ghidra crashes with a fatal JVM SIGSEGV after a specific Python script is executed. Once the affected script has been run, any subsequent Python script executed within the same Ghidra session causes Ghidra to crash. The issue reproduces consistently.

The crash is reproducible  with both Java 21 and Java 26.

The JVM crash log reports:

SIGSEGV (0xb)

Problematic frame:
C [libsystem_platform.dylib+0xac4] _platform_strlen+0x4

The crash happened outside the Java Virtual Machine in native code.

The fault address reported by the JVM is:

si_addr: Any heap address ( 0x0000000000000000 modification ), i.e. not a deterministic address.

When JVM core dumping is enabled, the crash produces a Java core dump at the time of the SIGSEGV.

which appears to be a NULL pointer dereference occurring in native code.

### To Reproduce
Open Ghidra.
Load a program into a project.
Execute the attached Python script from Script Manager.
Wait for the script to complete successfully.
Execute the same script again without restarting Ghidra.
Ghidra crashes with a fatal JVM error.

**Expected behavior:**

Python scripts should be executable multiple times within the same Ghidra session without causing a JVM crash.

**Actual behavior:**

The first execution succeeds.

The second execution of the same script causes a native SIGSEGV and terminates Ghidra.

## Problem

Maintainer-requested performance work is reducing repeated CPU, allocation, and filesystem work in OpenClaw's Node runtime. The campaign covers startup, warm Gateway requests, history processing, and streaming, with measured improvements landed through focused behavior tests, independent review, and required CI.

The campaign has now verified thirty-one landed performance PRs. The original four-PR stopping decision was too narrow; the broader measured sweep and its limitations are recorded below.

## Completed measured sweep

Thirty-one performance PRs are verified landed. Workspace inference #147144 merged as 47cb143799b9e8e59cec2b338d6d5af6bbfd1b04; its reviewed files, required CI, native landing and cleanup are verified. Its 256-agent lookup observations showed elapsed reductions of 33-68%, with adverse controls retained. Integration passed 34 tests after adapting to main's independent legacy-data-owner change.

Session context projection #147350 merged as 1c1affa936f63e04328630e88441d56f15b076d5. It passed 546 tests across 13 suites, 12 final selected checks and fresh P2 review. Both review-batch limitations and two unchanged provenance-file omissions remain explicit; separate owner inspection and existing tests cover those files. All 80 fixed timing windows preserved complete outputs. For 32 rows and 512 models, mean elapsed fell 35.26/31.88/50.33% for hit/miss/self-prefixed-miss, with corresponding CPU reductions of 34.07/26.58/48.28%. Exact-head CI passed with 116 successful jobs and 17 skips. Native landing and cleanup are complete; all ten changed landed files match the accepted integrated source.

Skill eligibility #147359 merged as af40e11dda8c7fa5251b1606812c0874ffcf9818. The refined candidate passed 119 tests across seven suites, production core typing and fresh P2 review. Its fixed original/candidate/candidate/original comparison matched all 12,288 outputs. For 64 skills, excluded preparation fell 98.27/98.70% and mixed preparation fell 57.90/62.48% for prompt/runtime entry points. No-binary controls improved about 27%; cached-positive means regressed 15.41/20.15% (about 0.021/0.030 ms per call), with opposite individual-pair directions. Adverse singleton controls remain disclosed. All five final focused checks passed after an equivalent test-only deferred-helper substitution, including the 19-test loader suite, format, lint, services test typing and diff check. Measured production differs from reviewed production only by removal of an unused initializer. Hosted review is clean. Exact-head CI passed with 116 successful jobs and 17 skips. Native landing and cleanup are complete; both landed files match the proved source.

The captured 8ba Gateway load completed its fixed operations without recorded request failures, but all readiness samples were degraded and maximum event-loop delay was 602.4 ms. The final pre-load sample was healthy. The earlier 120-second idle profile showed about 118.5 seconds of main-isolate idle while coarse process-tree CPU increased eight seconds. The completed profiler-off control recorded 1,000 ms of coarse CPU over 120,003.480 ms, with no driver requests, healthy readiness, normal exit and verified cleanup. Lower CPU is consistent with profiler overhead, but the runs were temporally separate across a WSL restart; cache/host state differed and whole-second counters can miss retired descendants. There is no exact causal attribution or retained-heap claim. No further idle profiling is selected.

Default source startup completed in 9.17 seconds. A normally installed package of the same captured source completed one empty-cache startup in 7,143.40 ms and one reused-cache startup in 5,391.42 ms. Both reached healthy/ready responses and exited cleanly; installed bytes were unchanged at verification. Coarse CPU was 7,000/5,000 ms and maximum root RSS 536.29/559.03 MiB. These are single instrumented observations, not statistical, OS-cold or causal speedup claims. The temporary package/cache later disappeared following a newly observed WSL boot; the initiator is unproven. Historical measurements remain valid, while those temporary files are no longer present.

SQLite child-cache recovery succeeded through the preserved built public SDK and frozen private dependencies. Four real snapshot calls preserved full typed/query/schema/source-byte results and cleaned up. Without propagation the child added no cache files; forwarding the parent's active cache directory populated 392 files and reused the unchanged set on the next call. Individual O1/C1/C2/O2 elapsed observations were 248.31/231.58/196.90/253.97 ms, retained only as mechanism observations. Exact-head CI passed with 118 successful jobs and 16 skips, and hosted review is clean. Native landing and cleanup are complete; both landed files match the proved source. All three changes are now counted as landed.


The current measured sweep is complete. A final read-only assessment at immutable main 23b3b7b9fcf6c70d8bcf79ca817de17caa62f2d7 found no further concrete small change supported by the retained workload evidence. History already reuses incremental projections and request-local byte counts; thinking projection already caches catalog and metadata lookups while preserving session-specific decisions; tool-schema checks surround distinct normalization and asynchronous materialization states. The earlier FTS cleanup and statement-cache candidates remain unsupported without changing their contracts. The retained load profile predates these final landings, so this is a bounded stopping decision for the audited paths, not a claim that future optimization is exhausted or a combined end-to-end speedup measurement.

## Landed improvements

- #146961: skip repeated fixed-context estimation when compaction has no pending text or images. The maintained large-tool-catalog experiment averaged 46.9% less estimation time and 46.0% less CPU, with complete budget parity and 50 existing tests passing. This is a synthetic owner measurement, not Gateway latency. Exact-head CI passed 114 jobs with 17 skips; source review, native merge and cleanup are verified. Landed as c1191cf5c9b29f617b765216b16ffa992a8bef09.
- #145680: accumulate incomplete usage records without repeatedly copying and searching the growing prefix; reuse cold SQLite transcript rows. A synthetic 8 MiB record scan changed from 120.43 to 19.93 ms on Windows Node 24.19.
- #145683: carry append facts from the shared stream merge owner and write complete SSE frames once. Stream corrections and protocol bytes remain covered.
- #145684: move Claude CLI project discovery off the event loop. With 1,001 synthetic projects, delay to an unrelated queued callback changed from 46.725 to 0.116 ms with roughly unchanged overall lookup time.
- #145696: reuse a normalized event's transcript path across subscribed history streams, with invalidation at the event boundary.
- #146031: avoid serialized role/text keys when merging imported chat histories. The full owner passed 20,044 output, identity, and immutability comparisons plus 140 focused tests.

- #146133: retain the lazily loaded Undici module at its existing owner, preserving overrides, failed-load retry, and the worker build adapter. Actual installed-Undici loopback requests and the worker build graph passed; full required CI passed.

- #146304: reject replies longer than any control token before uppercasing the growing buffer. The complete projector matched 1,994 original/native comparisons; 236 projection and registered agent-event tests and exact-head CI passed. - #146271: pass the validated channel selection into the existing status snapshot owner while retaining selected-account diagnostics. Selecting one of ten channels with 100 accounts each reduces inspections from 1,000 to 100. The original handler fails when an unrelated channel inspector throws; the candidate passed 272 focused tests and complete response comparisons, followed by 96 tests on its refreshed base. Proportional local checks, full exact-head CI and native landing passed; all six landed files match the reviewed source.
- #146467: avoid full skill inventory for ordinary URLs, Windows-style paths and escaped slashes when model aliases are configured. Independent review, seven refreshed guards, current-head CI and native landing passed. Both landed files match the reviewed bytes. Measurements use real stock discovery with primed caches and unrelated model application stubbed; the PR preserves the install-monitor exit uncertainty and independent readiness reconciliation.

- #146574: reuse request-local history byte counts during active-run recovery instead of serializing the full page again. Eight balanced processes completed 3,200 registered-handler requests with full response parity; active history/startup medians improved 28.63%/23.04%, with inactive elapsed controls within 1%. Eighty focused tests, fourteen selected checks, fresh review, full exact-head CI and all four hosted replay cases passed. Native landing is verified at 00fc6ce52e0d27362115bc10a81adf15d5ece7a9; all three landed files match reviewed bytes. Windows fixture-cleanup failures and supervisor corrections remain disclosed; measurements do not claim wire-transport or retained-memory gains.

These are operation-level measurements and behavior checks, not a claim that the whole Gateway is faster by the same percentage. Detailed evidence and limitations remain in each PR.

## Broader sweep results

- **Async skill preparation, #146373, landed:** native merge is `4e668c36a35223d431c3490e3874964a9c700b85`, from reviewed head `5f7b24ace4ecc9e7e5d27609e3968d70b4723fd9`. - **Real Gateway responsiveness:** four fresh fixed-count O,C,C,O processes compared `00fc6ce` and `ba0b96c` on WSL/Linux Node 24.19. - **Preserved async tradeoffs:** historical Windows snapshot-owner measurements verified complete snapshot/prompt/consumer parity and 23–29% earlier callbacks, with 21–33% more CPU and 14% more filesystem probes; same-key preparation was about 8% slower. The adaptive Gateway run handled roughly three times as many auxiliary probes, improved responsiveness and took 14–23% longer to complete combined work. Different RSS floors prevent a retained-memory claim. The initial candidate build failed its process-group cleanup gate; one ordinary full-build recovery passed. - **Disabled-plugin skill preparation, #146615, landed:** native merge `5606d86e838cb37d6c4e4121474f9f2fba2f86b0` matches both reviewed files. The existing owner skips metadata discovery when plugins are explicitly disabled while retaining cleanup of generated skill links. Fresh review, 79 owner/sibling tests, selected statics and full exact-head CI passed. Disabled fanout fell from 2.016 to 0.971 seconds (-51.8%); same-key preparation fell from 193.1 to 126.8 ms. An initial enabled-control slowdown did not consistently reproduce in a fixed O,C,C,O follow-up. Full consumer/publication parity held; both pilot and follow-up limitations remain in the PR. Native cleanup is verified.
- **Residual audit completed:** current source already defers heavy wizard and outbound adapters; worker initialization serves required recovery. The final candidate-only fixed-count CPU profile completed successfully. Binary path resolution/joining accounted for about 81 ms of 23.26 seconds of sampled intervals, which did not justify another refactor. Required parsing, serialization and live plugin-value behavior, plus existing watcher and concurrent database/Git work, yielded no additional supported patch.
- **Callback-access experiment held:** Node's filesystem Promise error handler appeared in the residual profile, motivating a one-file callback-access experiment. Fanout medians changed from 813 to 789 ms (-2.9%) and CPU from 1.210 to 1.163 seconds (-3.9%), with heavily overlapping ranges and later CPU pairs reversing direction. ## Candidates not being shipped

A no-underscore fast path at the control-token stripping owner passed 1,405 corpus cases and full output comparisons across 12 balanced processes, but ordinary-text and underscore controls showed unresolved regressions up to a 1.62 candidate/original median ratio. It is held. A memory-export experiment showed no consistent meaningful gain and is also held. Current profiles do not support optimizing the small routing-preparation allocation site. Transcript parsing, serialization, plugin value inspection and lazy imports remain visible allocation costs, but those costs alone do not establish avoidable work. Concurrent model-catalog, provider-metadata and SQLite work is excluded from duplicate implementation.

The allocation profile reports gross sampled allocations including collected objects, not retained memory. Earlier Gateway originals failed clean shutdown; those incomplete runs cannot support comparative claims. Shell line-ending and external entry-path assessment failures remain preserved; successful workloads were not repeated to replace them. Detailed raw evidence and qualifications stay with each PR and the local campaign record.

The campaign preserves streaming delivery, large snapshots, installed state and public contracts. It does not authorize live Gateway changes, new persistence/configuration policy, dependency changes or releases. Fifteen performance PRs were verified landed in the previous measured sweep.

At the maintainer's request, a further sweep is now active on fresh main f0817f23e939447755c614e29866b0467ee0d7c3, covering default Gateway startup, real CLI commands, periodic channel health work, host-thaw recovery and many stalled streaming subscribers. CPU profiles identified config schema preparation, command imports and plugin generation reference scanning for further work.

Channel owner diagnostics and four balanced timed processes preserve complete output parity: a health pass over 512 paused accounts fell from 523–734 ms to about 7.65 ms, and thaw recovery with 32 unrelated channels fell from 10–18 ms to 1.6–2.3 ms. Normal health timing was mixed, so this is a recovery-path result, not a general idle-CPU claim. The channel regression fails on original code and all 233 candidate tests pass across lifecycle, health-monitor and thaw suites. PR #146720 landed as 9ef7fb4ccc8f9f09dd2bd6c5331b7c0918e48da9 after all selected checks, fresh review and exact-head CI passed. This is the first performance PR landed in this continuation, bringing the campaign total to sixteen.

issue_description:
Linux 基础知识总结-目录操作-原文：

> mkdir [选项] 目录名：创建新目录（增）。例如：mkdir -m 755 my_directory，创建一个名为 my_directory 的新目录，并将其权限设置为 755，即所有用户对该目录有读、写和执行的权限。

755 权限的实际含义是：
​所有者（Owner）​: rwx（读、写、执行）
​所属组（Group）​: r-x（读、执行，​无写权限）
​其他用户（Others）​: r-x（读、执行，​无写权限）

该命令创建的目录并非所有用户都有写权限，只有所有者拥有完整权限，其他用户仅能读取和进入目录，但无法修改目录内容（如创建/删除文件）。若需要所有用户都有写权限，应设置为 ​777（rwxrwxrwx）。

issue_title: Control UI: add a global cross-agent session Watchlist
issue_description:
## Problem

Team Mode makes cross-agent sessions discoverable, but agent-specific pins do not provide one compact list of sessions currently being monitored across all agents.

For active multi-agent operations, users often need to watch a bespoke set of sessions regardless of ownership while preserving existing per-agent pin behavior.

## Proposed behavior

Add an independent global Watchlist state alongside the existing agent-specific pin:

- Existing pin remains scoped to the owning agent.
- A separate global watch action adds/removes a session from a **Watchlist** above all agent sections.
- A session may be agent-pinned, globally watched, both, or neither.
- Watchlist rows retain agent ownership, unread/running indicators, and normal click-to-open behavior.
- Watched sessions can be opened safely in cross-agent split panes.

The final iconography does not need to be a literal star plus pin; the two adjacent controls can look busy. The important requirement is independent agent-pin and global-watch state.

## Local prototype results

We implemented this on top of merged PR #141476 and tested it with 10 real agents and several hundred sessions:

- Cross-agent Watchlist rendered above agent sections.
- Sessions from multiple agents could be watched simultaneously.
- Watchlist membership persisted across hard refreshes.
- Watched sessions opened under the correct owning agent.
- Multiple watched sessions from different agents worked in split panes with independent composers/state.
- Existing agent pins remained independent.

## Data-model consideration

Team Mode currently loads a shared maximum of 300 sessions, with Gateway-pinned sessions prioritized. A browser-local Watchlist cannot render a watched session that falls outside that response window.

A production implementation may therefore need either:

1. Gateway-backed global watch state, with watched sessions prioritized in roster results, or
2. An explicit lookup/load path for watched session keys.

## Relationship to Team Mode

Merged PR #141476 solves cross-agent discovery and navigation. This proposal adds the compact operational view for “the sessions I am actively watching now,” independent of which agent owns them.

issue_title: 关于"HashMap 的长度为什么是 2 的幂次方"这个问题
issue_description:
> 我们首先可能会想到采用 % 取余的操作来实现。但是，重点来了：“取余(%)操作中如果除数是 2 的幂次则等价于与其除数减一的与(&)操作（也就是说 hash%length==hash&(length-1)的前提是 length 是 2 的 n 次方；）。” 并且 采用二进制位操作 & 相对于 % 能够提高运算效率，这就解释了 HashMap 的长度为什么是 2 的幂次方

除了上面所说的位运算比取余效率高之外，我觉得更重要的一个原因是，长度是2的幂次方，可以让HashMap在扩容的时候更均匀。例如:

- length = 8时，length - 1 = 7 的二进制位`0111`
- length = 16时，length - 1 = 15 的二进制位`1111`

这时候原本存在HashMap中的元素计算新的数组位置时 `hash&(length-1)`，取决hash的第四个二进制位（从右往左数），会出现两种情况：
1.  第四个二进制位为0，数组位置不变，也就是说当前元素在新数组和旧数组的位置相同
2. 第四个二进制位为1，数组位置在新数组扩容之后的那一部分

也就是说扩容之后，如果旧数组元素hash值比较均匀（至于hash值均不均匀，取决于前面讲的对象的hashcode()方法和扰动函数）的情况下，会有一半在新数组的前半部分，一半在新数组后半部分，这样达到一个均匀的效果

Affected project-side paths: `pkg/markdown/convert.go:16-38` (`ToHTML`, `html.WithUnsafe()`), `main.go:406-436` (`renderIndex`, writing `template.HTML(body)` verbatim into `out/index.html`), `main.go:310-356` + `tmpl/category-index.tmpl.html:113` (goquery href extraction → `{{.URL}}` + utm suffix). Affected dependency version: `github.com/yuin/goldmark >= 0, < 1.7.17` (fix: 1.7.17, commit `cb46bbc4eca29d55aa9721e04ad207c23ccc44f9`). Audit baseline: main branch commit `2222bc3e8d6af0a969a37640909413bf259ef235` (2026-09-07). ## Weakness Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (Cross-site Scripting) (cwe-79) — on the dependency side, improper neutralization of URL schemes (the IsDangerousURL check runs before character-reference resolution, so the scheme filter is bypassed by entity encoding) ## Description > **Version declaration:** This report targets the **avelino/awesome-go main @ `2222bc3e8d6af0a969a37640909413bf259ef235`** repository tree together with **github.com/yuin/goldmark v1.6.0** (pinned by go.mod); advisory **CVE-2026-5160 / GHSA-c97m-vxhj-p7j6 / GO-2026-5320** (affected symbols: `renderer/html` `renderLink`, `renderImage`, `renderAutoLink`; the advisory JSON is archived as `GO-2026-5320.json`). The findings are **code-level white-box confirmations** (both-sides source diff + dependency-level differential repro + full-pipeline twin builds); no live-service requests were performed in this submission. ### Summary goldmark v1.6.0's `renderer/html` renders links/images by performing the `IsDangerousURL` prefix check on the **raw bytes first**, and only resolving character references later when writing, via `util.URLEscape(dest, true)` — the order is inverted. The raw bytes of `javascript:alert(1)`, `javascript:...`, and `javascript:...` never start with `javascript:`, so they pass the prefix check; afterwards `:`/`:`/`:` are resolved to `:` and the executable scheme is written verbatim into the href/src attribute. The fixed v1.7.17 computes `dest := util.URLEscape(n.Destination, true)` first and only then calls `IsDangerousURL(dest)` (diff: `goldmark-html.go-v1.6.0-vs-v1.7.17.patch`). Two independent project-side facts compound this: ① the production configuration enables `html.WithUnsafe()` (`convert.go:24`), which short-circuits the entire check (`if r.Unsafe || !IsDangerousURL(...)`) — **nothing is filtered even without a bypass**; ② `main.go` `renderIndex` (:406-436) writes the goldmark output verbatim into `out/index.html` via `template.HTML(body)`, and goquery `extractCategory` (:310-356) lifts href attributes into the `category-index.tmpl.html:113` sink ``, with no project-side scheme validation anywhere on the path. Whether viewed from the dependency's default configuration or the production configuration, attacker README links with entity-encoded `javascript:` schemes land in the deployed site. ### Finding A: v1.6.0 checks before entity resolution — the root of the bypass **Files (dependency side):** goldmark v1.6.0 `renderer/html/html.go:632-640` (`renderLink`; same shape `renderImage` :676-684) ```go _, _ = w.WriteString("`. The trailing `//` of `javascript:alert(1)//` JS-comments out the appended utm query; a click executes. - Key fact (recorded honestly): under the production configuration (`WithUnsafe`) goldmark performs **no** URL filtering at all — even the plain `javascript:alert(4)` control passes; the CVE bypass means the dependency is unsafe **even in the default safe configuration** (without `WithUnsafe`), and only ≥ 1.7.17 restores a working filter. Both facts are reproduced. ### Finding C: Dependency-level differential repro and full-pipeline artifacts **Files (evidence):** `minrepro-goldmark-v1.6.0-output.txt`, `minrepro-goldmark-v1.7.17-output.txt`, `sinkA_index_fragment.txt`, `sinkB_category_fragment.txt`, `browser_view_audit.txt` Differential repro (goldmark v1.6.0 invoked through the real project package `pkg/markdown.ToHTML` vs a twin module at v1.7.17; the emitted HTML is re-parsed with `golang.org/x/net/html` — the same attribute entity-decoding a browser performs): | payload | v1.6.0 safe-mode (IsDangerousURL active) | v1.6.0 production (WithUnsafe) | v1.7.17 safe-mode | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `[x](javascript:alert(1)//)` | href="javascript:alert(1)//" **DANGEROUS (bypass)** | DANGEROUS | href="" BLOCKED | | `[x](javascript:alert(2)//)` | **bypass** | DANGEROUS | BLOCKED | | `[x](javascript:alert(3)//)` | **bypass** | DANGEROUS | BLOCKED | | `[x](javascript:alert(4))` plain | href="" BLOCKED (control) | DANGEROUS | BLOCKED | | `![x](javascript:alert(5))` image | src="javascript:alert(5)" **bypass (renderImage)** | DANGEROUS | BLOCKED | Full-pipeline build (`go run .`, AWESOME_SKIP_FETCH=1) confirms the deployed artifacts: 1. **Sink A:** `out/index.html` contains ``, `(2)//`, `(3)//`, `javascript:alert(4)`, and `` (`sinkA_index_fragment.txt`). 2. **Sink B:** `out/poc-goldmark-entity-scheme-category/index.html` contains `` (`sinkB_category_fragment.txt`); the `//` comments out the utm suffix and a click executes. issue_title: Statusline badge breaks after a plugin update: the nudge points at the versioned plugin cache
issue_description:
## What happens

On native Claude Code, the first `SessionStart` nudges the agent to add this to `settings.json` (`hooks/ponytail-activate.js`):

```json
"statusLine": { "type": "command", "command": "bash \"<plugin root>/hooks/ponytail-statusline.sh\"" }
```

`<plugin root>` is Claude Code's plugin cache, which is versioned:

```
~/.claude/plugins/cache/<marketplace>/ponytail/4.12.0/hooks/ponytail-statusline.sh
```

When the plugin updates, Claude Code installs `4.13.0/` and removes the old version directory. The `statusLine` command now points at a file that no longer exists, so the `[PONYTAIL]` badge disappears without any error. The nudge never comes back: `activate` only checks that `settings.statusLine` is set, and `.ponytail-statusline-nudged` is already written.

## Repro

1. Install ponytail from a marketplace, accept the statusline setup. The badge shows.
2. Update the plugin to a newer version (or wait for auto-update) and start a new session after the old cache directory is cleaned up.
3. The badge is gone. `ls` on the path in `settings.json` gives `No such file or directory`.

I hit exactly this on my machine with another plugin that uses the same pattern: its `statusLine` pointed at `cache/<mkt>/<plugin>/84cc3c14fa1e/...`, and only `2.7.0/` was left in the cache. The ponytail nudge builds the path the same way (`path.join(__dirname, scriptName)`).

## Possible fix

- **Stable path:** `activate` copies the statusline script to `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/ponytail-statusline.sh` (`.ps1` on Windows) and the nudge points there. Each session refreshes the copy, so it survives updates. `uninstall.js` removes it.
- **Recover broken setups:** if `settings.statusLine.command` references a `ponytail-statusline` script that no longer exists, nudge once with the stable path, even when `.ponytail-statusline-nudged` already exists.

Happy to send a PR for both if that direction works for you.

### Bug Description

On self-hosted instances with a large usable-credentials set (~2k), opening the Node Details View (NDV) for credential-using nodes (e.g. OpenAI Chat Model) freezes the UI for many seconds (observed ~5–22s).

Chrome Performance profiling shows the cost is almost entirely **frontend main-thread work** inside `useNodeCredentialOptions` during the `dblclick` handler — not network, database, or workflow size.

Hot path:
1. `getCredentialOptions` builds dropdown options with `{...option}` over **Vue reactive** usable credentials, which tracks every field.
2. `isCredentialExisting` rebuilds that full options list just to check one credential id.

This scales with instance usable-credentials size. A smaller instance on the same build (~600 credentials) does not show the lag. Reproduced on a brand-new empty workflow with only a newly added OpenAI Chat Model node.

### Proposed fix

PR: https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/pull/40198

- Spread `toRaw(option)` when building options
- O(1) `usableCredentials` map lookup for existence checks
- Keep `overrideCredentials` path for Instance AI

### To Reproduce

2. Open any workflow (even empty).
3. Add OpenAI Chat Model (or another credential-using node).
4. Double-click the node to open NDV.
5. Observe multi-second UI freeze before the panel is usable.
6. Optional: Chrome Performance → record the dblclick; expect a long `EventDispatch` dominated by JS in the credential-options path.

issue_title: [Bug]: ponytail does not detect caveman conflict — both inject contradictory instructions
issue_description:
## Bug Description

When ponytail and caveman are both active, they both inject `additionalContext` on `UserPromptSubmit`. The model receives two contradictory style instruction sets every turn:

- Caveman: `"CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE (full). Drop articles/filler/pleasantries/hedging. Fragments OK."`
- Ponytail: `"PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE (full). The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first."`

Previous issues (#18, #68, #193) asked "can they coexist?" and were closed with "yes, they stack". But the **actual bug** is that both plugins inject per-turn style reminders simultaneously, causing the model to receive contradictory instructions about output style. This results in unpredictable, inconsistent outputs.

## What caveman already does

Caveman PR [#577](https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/pull/577) added conflict detection: when ponytail (or other compression plugins) is detected in `settings.json`, caveman reduces its per-turn injection to a one-liner instead of the full ruleset. But ponytail does NOT reciprocate — it always injects its full ruleset regardless of whether caveman is active.

## Proposed Fix

In `ponytail-mode-tracker.js`, before emitting the per-turn `additionalContext`, check `settings.json` for known compression plugins (caveman, etc.). If detected, reduce the per-turn injection to a minimal one-liner:

```
PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE (full) — reduced injection (another compression plugin detected). Ponytail rules still apply per SessionStart injection.
```

The SessionStart full ruleset is unchanged — ponytail rules still apply, just the per-turn reinforcement is reduced to avoid contradictory instructions.

This mirrors the approach caveman already uses in its `detectCompressionConflict()` function.

## Testing

With caveman installed in settings.json:
- **Before**: model receives both `"CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE (full). Drop articles..."` AND `"PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE (full). The ladder enforced..."` every turn → contradictory instructions
- **After**: model receives `"CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE (full) — reduced injection"` + ponytail full injection = no contradiction

issue_title: [Feature Request] Ponytail Debugger Skill
issue_description:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Ponytail's ability to pinpoint root causes with the audit skill, as well as PR review skill is almost perfect to how a real senior dev does. I would love to apply this mental model of problem solving to a debugging skill, where I can give ponytail logs and code, and have it debug errors. 

**Proposed Solution**
Introduce a dedicated `/ponytail debug` mode (or sub-skill) that forces the agent to climb a Debugging Decision Ladder before modifying any code:

1. **Reproduction First:** Create or run a minimal reproduction case (e.g., single unit test or isolated script) to confirm the failure.
2. **Root Cause Isolation:** Identify the exact line or condition triggering the bug—do not assume adjacent architecture is broken.
3. **Surgical Patch:** Apply the smallest valid diff (preferring a 1-to-2 line guard or logical fix over a refactor).
4. **Scope Lockdown:** Strictly prohibit refactoring surrounding code, modifying working abstractions, or adding external libraries while fixing the issue.

**Context / Examples**
* **Default Agent Behavior:** Replaces a 15-line custom date-parsing helper with a 120-line utility module and a new dependency just to fix an unhandled `null` input.
* **Expected Ponytail Debug Behavior:** Adds `if (!input) return null;`, runs the test, verifies the fix, and stops.

**Acceptance Criteria**
* [ ] Add `/ponytail debug` command and `PONYTAIL_MODE=debug` environment configuration.
* [ ] Update canonical `SKILL.md` ruleset with the explicit Debug Decision Ladder.
* [ ] Maintain strict boundary protection (do not simplify away security, accessibility, or error-handling checks during bug fixes).

issue_title: Support Atom Feeds
issue_description:
<!-- Describe this new feature. Think about if it really belongs in the Hugo core module; you may want to discuss it on https://discourse.gohugo.io/ first.  -->

Currently, Hugo only supports [RSS feeds](https://gohugo.io/templates/rss/) (see: [template file](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/master/tpl/tplimpl/embedded/templates/rss.xml)).
It would be nice if Atom feeds as well, as Atom feels like a much more 'sane' format.

See [here](https://www.intertwingly.net/wiki/pie/Rss20AndAtom10Compared) for a comparison between RSS and Atom.
Some notable ones:
- you technically should *not* provide html content in an RSS feed, and instead only provide plain text content (see: [w3c feed validator](https://validator.w3.org/feed/docs/)), whereas an Atom feed allows you to use plain text, HTML, XHTML, and more (& specify which one it is).
- RSS feeds only include a summary (the `<description>` element) of the article rather than the entire article, like Atom does. (see: #4071)
- RSS has some weird specific not-hard-requirements-but-recommendations, for example when specifying the author, you should format it as "[email address] ([name of person])" (see: [w3c feed validator](https://validator.w3.org/feed/docs/))
- the spec for RSS is rather vague, whereas Atom has an official RFC
- RSS has some weird/undocumented fields like `<ttl>` (recommended to avoid using), `<cloud>` (no documentation on how the server should be implemented for this), `<textInput>` (how this should be used is entirely undocumented)

A lot of these differences are caused by RSS being something that is used by a ton of applications who all did different things, and a ton of its "spec" is defined by convention and how other people use it.

References/Useful Resources:
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4287
- http://www.atomenabled.org/developers/protocol/
- https://validator.w3.org/feed/docs/atom.html


I'd be willing to contribute a template for an Atom feed later, if open to it being added.

issue_title: Ruleset fights host plan/review gates (agent writes spec .md instead of submit_plan)
issue_description:
## Found while using ponytail in OpenCode

**Symptom:** with a plan/review mode active and the plan-review tool available (`submit_plan` in OpenCode), the agent rarely opens it — it ships code, or writes hand-made `.md` / prose summaries instead.

**Root cause (forensic):**

1. `grep submit_plan` across the repo returns nothing — the ruleset never acknowledges host review gates.
2. Two rules actively clash with plan mode:
   - "Code first." (Output section)
   - "Ship the lazy version ... Never stall on an answer you can default" (Rules)
   
   The ruleset is injected last into the system prompt every turn, so it wins over the host's plan-only constraint.
3. The one-check rule pushes toward writing files; in plan mode the only permitted write is an `.md`, which explains the spec-file behavior.
4. Note: the ponytail MCP server only serves the ruleset text; MCP being active has no bearing on whether `submit_plan` gets used — that's a host tool.

**Secondary finding:** the runnable-check rule never bounds execution, so checks that fail due to a timeout (not logic) get re-run endlessly against long-running commands.

Proposed fix incoming as a PR: scope both rules to execution choices, add an explicit plan-gate clause, and require one bounded check run.

issue_title: ponytail-debt: grep pattern misses C-style block comments (/* ponytail: ... */)
issue_description:
## What happened

`ponytail-debt`'s SKILL.md documents this scan command:

```
grep -rnE '(#|//) ?ponytail:' .
```

This only matches line comments (`#`, `//`). It silently misses a `ponytail:` marker written as a C-style block comment, e.g. in TS/JS/CSS:

```ts
/* ponytail: cartId isn't used to tailor results yet — no upsell-selection
   business logic (e.g. related-by-collection, merchant-configured picks)
   has been specified. Upgrade path: read a merchant-configured upsell
   list once admin-api exposes one. */
```

Running `/ponytail-debt` against a repo containing only that marker reports `No ponytail: debt. Clean ledger.` even though a real, correctly-formatted shortcut comment exists — the exact "later means never" rot the skill is supposed to catch.

## Repro

1. Add a `ponytail:` marker as a `/* ... */` block comment (rather than `//`) anywhere in a repo.
2. Run `/ponytail-debt`.
3. Expected: 1 marker found. Actual: "No ponytail: debt. Clean ledger."

## Suggested fix

Extend the alternation to include the block-comment opener:

```
grep -rnE '(#|//|/\*) ?ponytail:' .
```

Verified this catches the block-comment case above without introducing false positives on a real repo (still 0 hits on files that don't contain the marker).

## Evidence

Found while running `/ponytail-audit` → `/ponytail-debt` in a session against a real TS/JS monorepo; the block-comment marker was independently visible in the project's own wiki docs (which referenced "the `ponytail:` comment in `product/resolvers.ts`"), which is what surfaced the grep miss.

**Bug**

`ponytail-mcp/index.js:12` passes `version: "0.1.0"` to the `McpServer` constructor:

```javascript
const server = new McpServer({ name: "ponytail", version: "0.1.0" });
```

However, `ponytail-mcp/package.json` declares `"version": "4.8.4"`. MCP clients that inspect the server version see a stale `0.1.0`, and this will need manual updating on every release — something easy to forget.

**Fix**

Read the version from `package.json` at startup:

```javascript
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
const { version } = JSON.parse(readFileSync(new URL('./package.json', import.meta.url), 'utf8'));
const server = new McpServer({ name: "ponytail", version });
```

Or use a `createRequire`-based import if consistency with the other adapters matters.

issue_title: [Bug] /ponytail never sets a mode in Claude Code: the UserPromptSubmit hook receives the SKILL.md body, not the command text
issue_description:
# [Bug] `/ponytail` never sets a mode in Claude Code: the UserPromptSubmit hook receives the SKILL.md body, not the command text

## Summary

In Claude Code, `/ponytail` is dispatched as a **skill**, not as a `commands/*.md` slash command. The harness therefore hands `UserPromptSubmit` a `data.prompt` that begins with `<command-message>` / `<command-name>` tags and then contains **the entire body of `skills/ponytail/SKILL.md`** — not the literal string `/ponytail:ponytail`.

`hooks/ponytail-mode-tracker.js:23` tests:

```js
if (/^[/@$]ponytail/.test(prompt)) {
```

That anchor never matches, so `setMode()` is never called, `~/.claude/.ponytail-active` is never written, and everything that reads it (`ponytail-instructions.js`, `ponytail-subagent.js`, the statusline) sees no active mode.

This is the same root cause as the (now fixed) #161, seen from the other side. Before #162 landed, the old deactivation regex

```js
if (/\b(stop ponytail|normal mode)\b/i.test(prompt)) {
```

matched ponytail's **own** SKILL.md, which says on line 29:

> `unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.`

So invoking `/ponytail:ponytail` printed `PONYTAIL MODE OFF`. The skill disabled itself by reading itself. #162's `isDeactivationCommand` fixed that half; the command-detection half is still open.

## Environment

- ponytail **4.8.4** (marketplace `DietrichGebert/ponytail`, user scope)
- Claude Code CLI **2.1.206**, Linux
- Hook wired via `hooks/claude-codex-hooks.json` → `UserPromptSubmit` → `ponytail-mode-tracker.js`

## Reproduction

1. Install ponytail 4.8.4 in Claude Code, start a session.
2. Invoke `/ponytail:ponytail` (or `/ponytail full`) from the slash menu.
3. Observe: no `PONYTAIL MODE CHANGED` output from the hook.
4. `ls ~/.claude/.ponytail-active` → **No such file or directory**.

On 4.2.0, step 3 instead prints `PONYTAIL MODE OFF`, every single time.

Typing `ponytail ultra` as ordinary prose still works, because then `data.prompt` really is the literal text. Only the slash/skill path is affected — which is the documented way to use it.

## Why this wasn't caught

#269 reported the `commands/*.toml` vs `commands/*.md` mismatch and was closed unmerged, with:

> the `UserPromptSubmit` hook (`ponytail-mode-tracker.js`) parses the prompt text, so `/ponytail ultra` persists the mode whether it came from a skill or was typed raw. It even handles the `/ponytail:ponytail` form.

The code does handle that form. The harness just never delivers it: when the command comes from a skill, the prompt is the skill body. The skills *do* show up in the `/` menu with their arg hints, as you observed — that part is orthogonal, and it's what makes the failure invisible. The menu entry works; the hook behind it doesn't.

## Suggested fix

Prefer the `<command-name>` tag when present, and fall back to the raw prompt otherwise. Claude Code emits a `<command-args>` tag for at least some commands (empty when there is no argument); the snippet below tolerates its absence:

```js
const raw = data.prompt || '';
const name = raw.match(/<command-name>\s*([^<]+?)\s*<\/command-name>/)?.[1];
const args = raw.match(/<command-args>\s*([^<]*?)\s*<\/command-args>/)?.[1];
const prompt = (name ? `${name} ${args ?? ''}` : raw).trim().toLowerCase();
```

Everything downstream (`^[/@$]ponytail`, the `parts[0]` / `parts[1]` split, `isDeactivationCommand`) then works unchanged, and `isDeactivationCommand` keeps protecting the raw-prose path.

Worth a regression test that feeds the tracker a `data.prompt` built from the real skill body: it fails on both counts today (no activation; and on any build predating #162, a spurious deactivation).
