issue_description:
### Want to Contribute?

This issue is part of the **Contributor Sprint** initiative. To work on it:

1. Join our Discord: https://chat.freecodecamp.org
2. Claim the **Naomi's Sprints** role
3. Ping Naomi in `#naomis-sprints` to be assigned this ticket

### Describe the Issue

The Graphs and Trees review has inaccurate definitions, missing concepts from its source material, and formatting problems:

1. The frontmatter title does not match the block metadata or intro entry.

   > `title: Review Graphs and Trees`

2. Several concepts do not use the review format of a bold term followed by a colon and an explanation. Some entries are plain labels, nested fragments, or unlabeled statements.

   > `- Directed: edges have a direction (from one node to another), often represented with straight lines and arrows.`
   >
   > `- **Breadth-First Search (BFS)**`
   >
   > `- **Adjacency List**`
   >
   > `- They have no loops or cycles (paths where the start and end nodes are the same).`
   >
   > `- Max-Heap`

3. The DAG entry defines only an acyclic graph. It does not state that a DAG is directed.

   > `- Acyclic (DAG): does not contain cycles.`

4. The disconnected graph definition treats the absence of a direct edge between two nodes as disconnection. Two nodes can lack a direct edge and still have a path between them.

   > `- Disconnected: contains two or more nodes that are not connected by any edges.`

5. The traversal section omits visited-node tracking, queue and stack mechanics, memory use, connected-component detection, and the shortest-path limitation of DFS.

   > `- **Breadth-First Search (BFS)**`
   > `  - Uses a queue.`
   > `  - Explores level by level.`
   > `  - Finds shortest path in unweighted graphs.`
   >
   > `- **Depth-First Search (DFS)**`
   > `  - Uses a stack (or recursion).`
   > `  - Explores a branch fully before backtracking.`
   > `  - Useful for cycle detection and path finding.`

6. The breadth-first search entry covers graph nodes but omits the state-space technique taught in the workshop. That workshop tracks a partial string and counts of opening and closing parentheses, then enqueues only states that can still produce a balanced result.

   > `- **Breadth-First Search (BFS)**`
   > `  - Uses a queue.`
   > `  - Explores level by level.`
   > `  - Finds shortest path in unweighted graphs.`

7. The graph representation section omits weighted and unweighted matrix values, self-loops, adjacency-list implementations, dense and sparse graph tradeoffs, and the time and space complexities taught in the source lesson.

   > `- **Adjacency List**`
   > `  - Each node has a list of its neighbors.`
   > `  - Space efficient for sparse graphs.`
   > `  - Easy to iterate over neighbors.`
   >
   > `- **Adjacency Matrix**`
   > `  - A 2D array where rows and columns represent nodes.`
   > `  - Space intensive for large graphs.`
   > `  - Fast to check if an edge exists between two nodes.`

8. The review does not cover the weighted shortest-path algorithm taught in the workshop. The missing concepts include an adjacency matrix, `Infinity` for missing edges, distance, path, and visited arrays, selection of the closest unvisited node, edge relaxation, unreachable nodes, and an optional target.

   > `- Weighted: edges have weights (values) associated with them, that can be used to perform arithmetic operations.`
   >
   > `- Finds shortest path in unweighted graphs.`

9. The tree section omits hierarchy terminology, node measurements, subtrees, balanced trees, and the AVL, red-black, and B-tree types introduced in the source lesson.

   > `- They have no loops or cycles (paths where the start and end nodes are the same).`
   > `- They must be connected (every node can be reached from every other node).`
   >
   > `### Common types of trees`
   >
   > `- Binary Trees`
   > `  - Each node has at most two children, a left and a right child.`
   >
   > `- Binary Search Trees (BST)`
   > `  - A binary tree in which every left child is less than its parent, and every right child is greater than its parent.`

10. The binary search tree definition applies its ordering rule only to immediate children. The rule applies to every value in both subtrees, and each subtree must also be a binary search tree.

    > `- A binary tree in which every left child is less than its parent, and every right child is greater than its parent.`

11. The tree subheading is not in title case.

    > `### Common types of trees`

12. The trie section omits the empty root, prefix paths, end-of-word markers, insertion of missing characters, and memory costs for strings with many unique characters. Its complexity notation is also missing inline-code formatting.

    > `Also known as prefix trees, they are used to store sets of strings, where each node represents a character.`
    >
    > `Shared prefixes are stored only once, making them efficient for tasks like autocomplete and spell checking.`
    >
    > `Search and insertion operations have a time complexity of O(L), where L is the length of the string.`

13. The priority queue section states that higher-priority elements always come first, although an implementation can remove either the highest-priority or lowest-priority element first. It does not account for insertion order when priorities tie, and it omits the applications taught in the source lesson.

    > `Standard queues follow FIFO (First In First Out) and stacks follow LIFO (Last In First Out). However, in a priority queue, elements with higher priority are served before those with lower priority, regardless of their insertion order.`

14. The heap section omits complete binary trees, array storage, parent and child indexes, core heap operations, bubble-up and bubble-down behavior, comparison callbacks, stable tie breaking, and operation complexities.

    > `- Max-Heap`
    > `  - The value of each parent node is greater than or equal to the values of its children.`
    > `  - The largest element is at the root.`
    >
    > `- Min-Heap`
    > `  - The value of each parent node is less than or equal to the values of its children.`
    > `  - The smallest element is at the root.`
    >
    > `JavaScript doesn't have a built-in heap module, but you can implement a min-heap using an array.`

15. The heap definition begins with a pronoun that has no noun antecedent.

    > `It's a specialized tree-based data structure with a very specific property called the heap property.`

16. The weighted graph sentence has a comma that separates a restrictive clause from the noun it modifies.

    > `- Weighted: edges have weights (values) associated with them, that can be used to perform arithmetic operations.`

17. The application list has no conjunction before its final item.

    > `Graphs are used in various applications such as maps, networks, recommendation systems, dependency resolution.`

18. The assignment capitalizes common nouns as if they were part of a title.

    > `Review the Graphs and Trees topics and concepts.`

### Affected Pages

https://www.freecodecamp.org/learn/javascript-v9/review-graphs-and-trees-js/review-graphs-and-trees-js

### Expected behavior

The review should accurately summarize the graph and tree concepts introduced by the module's lecture and workshops. Its definitions should distinguish graph connectivity, directed acyclic graphs, binary search tree ordering, and configurable priority queue behavior.

The graph sections should cover BFS and DFS mechanics and tradeoffs, state-space search, graph representation formats and complexities, and weighted shortest-path processing. The tree sections should cover hierarchy terms, measurements, balancing, tree types, trie structure and costs, and heap storage, operations, ordering, and complexities.

Each review concept should use a bold term followed by a colon and an explanation. Headings should use title case, code and complexity notation should use inline-code formatting, and the remaining grammar and title inconsistencies should be corrected.

issue_title: Implement a Stack: peek tests accept changes to the collection
issue_description:
### Describe the Issue

The Implement a Stack lab includes this hint:

> `` `peek` function should return the top element of the stack without removing it. ``

The test pushes `'first'` and `'second'`, then calls `peek(stack)` twice and checks that both calls return `'second'`. It never checks that the collection remains unchanged.

Replacing the reference solution's `peek` function with this incorrect implementation passes all 16 extracted test bodies in a targeted Node.js reproduction:

```js
function peek(stack) {
  if (stack.collection.length > 1) stack.collection.shift();
  return stack.collection[0];
}
```

The first call removes `'first'`, leaving `['second']`. Both calls still return `'second'`, so the test accepts a function that discards part of the stack. The reproduction used Node assertion adapters for the Chai assertions, rather than the curriculum runner.

### Affected Pages

https://www.freecodecamp.org/learn/javascript-v9/lab-implement-a-stack/implement-a-stack

### Expected behavior

The tests should verify that `peek` returns the top element while preserving the entire collection, including its length, values, and order. An implementation that removes or changes any stack element should fail.

issue_title: deploySegments
issue_description:
**What am I proposing?**

Currently Hugo has [renderSegments](https://gohugo.io/configuration/segments/). I'd like to propose similar functionality for deploy, a `--deploySegments` flag on the hugo deploy command.

**Why?**

Mostly for smarter informed deploy, typically there might be some logic or trigger for a build. Maybe in a normal scenario you might render segment1,segment2 and you could just hugo deploy that as it only exists in the public dir. You would have to do some careful includes,excludes or maxdeletes 0 to make sure its not removing non segments in the remote... but with a deploy segments command you would just run the deploy command with the same segments for deploy

**How might it work?**

Ideally it would mirror the functionality. For example you could run something like below and it would understand the segment concept from the config and which of the built files in `./public` are appropriate to deploy.

```
hugo deploy --deploySegments segment1
```

A few things come to mind though:

One of the issues with this is at deploy time it has no concept of the relationship between the segment (source md) files and the output (built html) files. It only has the built files to deal with.

Some thoughts on that:
- Try and infer the relationship based on path or other telltale signs although its probably error prone
- Generate a “segment outputs” manifest during the build or a separate command in hugo. This would output a mapping of segment -> built files in a json file in the public folder that could be read during deploy time. The deploy function would treat this almost as if these are the only files in the public folder so you could still do include/exclude logic etc on top if desired.

**Alternatives**

- Manually use includes/excludes on the deploy config to map your understanding of the built files that map to what you want?
- Other deploy tools?

issue_title: Feature: add a `reuse` tag to ponytail-review/audit for in-repo duplication (ladder rung 2 at review time)
issue_description:
## Background

The ladder used at write time (`skills/ponytail/SKILL.md`) has rung 2, "Already in this codebase? Reuse it, don't re-write it." (added via #253, following #217).

But `ponytail-review` and `ponytail-audit` — the skills that check code *after* it's written, on a diff or on the whole repo — only have five tags: `delete`, `stdlib`, `native`, `yagni`, `shrink`. None of them cover "this new helper duplicates one that already exists elsewhere in this same repo." So the write-time rung has no corresponding check-time tag: if a helper gets duplicated anyway, review/audit currently has nothing to catch it with.

## Observed case

We had a session that self-reported adding 4 small helpers, although equivalent helpers already existed in the same repo (a Python/JS monorepo). Running the current review tags over that diff would not have flagged it — none of `delete/stdlib/native/yagni/shrink` matches "equivalent code already exists elsewhere in this repo."

## Proposal

Add a sixth tag to both `skills/ponytail-review/SKILL.md` and `skills/ponytail-audit/SKILL.md`:

- `reuse:` an equivalent function/script/config already exists in this repo at `<path>`. Replacement: point to it.

And add one line to the instructions in both skills: "Search the same repo for an existing equivalent before flagging or accepting a new helper."

## Local workaround

Until then, we append one line to the review prompt ourselves: "Search the same repo for an existing equivalent (function/script/config); if found, list it as reuse."

Happy to send a PR if the direction is welcome.

issue_title: Postgres node over SSH tunnel hangs indefinitely after the shared SSH client is closed
issue_description:
### Bug Description

Postgres nodes using an SSH-tunnelled credential can hang forever. They never error and never retry, and `retryOnFail` / `onError: continueErrorOutput` don't fire. Only the workflow timeout or a manual cancel stops them. While it's hanging, nothing reaches the SSH server or the database.

It happens when two Postgres nodes with different `typeVersion`s (e.g. 2.5 and 2.6) use the same SSH credential:

- `ConnectionPoolManager` keys pools by node version, so they get **two pools**.
- `SSHClientsManager` keys SSH clients by host/user/key only, so both pools **share one SSH client**.

Only the pool that created the SSH client is subscribed to its lifecycle (the `existing` branch in `SSHClientsManager.getClient` ignores the caller's `abortController`).

When that pool is evicted after its 5-min TTL, its abort closes the shared SSH client while the other pool is still using it. The surviving pool keeps the closed client. The next query connects to the local TCP proxy, and `sshClient.forwardOut()` throws `Error: Not connected` synchronously (ssh2 1.15.0, `lib/client.js:1401`) inside the proxy's `connection` listener. That throw ends up in the global `uncaughtException` handler. The accepted socket is never piped or destroyed, so pg waits on it forever.

Two related details:

- The node's `connectionTimeout` option doesn't help, because it isn't part of the pool cache key. A pool keeps the timeout of whichever node created it.
- The `forwardOut` error-callback path has the same socket leak: it closes the proxy server but not the socket it already accepted.


### To Reproduce

1. Create a Postgres credential with SSH Tunnel enabled.
2. Workflow A: Postgres node `typeVersion` 2.5, Execute Query `SELECT 1`. Workflow B: Postgres node `typeVersion` 2.6, `SELECT 1`.
3. Run A once, then B within a few seconds. B reuses A's SSH client, and the SSH server shows only one session.
4. Keep running B every ~30s. Don't run A again.
5. About 5 min after A's last run, A's pool is evicted and the SSH session closes. Every following run of B hangs, and `Error: Not connected` is reported as an uncaught exception.

We reproduced this on `n8nio/n8n:2.41.4` against a local `postgres:16` and an OpenSSH server, using n8n's compiled `SSHClientsManager` and `configurePostgres`. Excerpt:

```
[t+272.5s] B (v2.6): ok (174ms)
[t+300.3s] ConnectionPoolManager: Found stale pool. Cleaning it up.
[t+300.3s] Got abort signal, cleaning up ssh client.
[t+302.5s] uncaughtException: Not connected
[t+322.6s] B (v2.6, connectionTimeout 10): HUNG (no result after 20s)
... every later query: "Not connected" + hang

### Expected behavior

If the tunnel is gone, the query should fail promptly with an error, so retries and error outputs work. The next execution should open a fresh SSH connection.


### Debug Info

- n8n version: 2.41.4 (n8n Cloud)
- ssh2: 1.15.0
- Database: PostgreSQL 16 (AWS RDS) behind an OpenSSH bastion

### Operating System

n8n cloud

### n8n Version

2.41.4

### Node.js Version

26.7.0

### Database

PostgreSQL

### Execution mode

main (default)

### Hosting

n8n cloud

issue_title: [Performance]: doctor --fix takes many minutes with large agent DB while integrity checks complete in <1s
issue_description:
## Summary

`openclaw doctor --fix` can take many minutes on an otherwise healthy installation when one agent SQLite database is large.

In the observed case, the main agent database is approximately 715 MiB. `doctor --fix` had been running for more than 9 minutes while consuming very little CPU.

The surprising part is that the actual database integrity validation of the 715 MiB database completes in less than one second. Most of the wall-clock time appears to be spent later in serial database maintenance, registration, revision/content-version checks, state writes, leases, and plugin migration work.

During this time the managed Gateway is stopped, so the excessive Doctor duration also becomes Gateway downtime.

## Environment

- OpenClaw: `2026.9.8 (fc23bc8)`
- Installation: npm global
- OS: macOS 27.0.1
- Architecture: arm64
- Node: 24.18.1
- Command:

```bash
openclaw doctor --fix
```

Agent/state database sizes:

```text
715M  ~/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
15M   ~/.openclaw/agents/runpod-qwen-a40/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
704K  ~/.openclaw/agents/openclaw/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
45M   ~/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite
```

## Observed behavior

The Doctor process was still running after more than nine minutes:

```text
PID    %CPU  %MEM  ELAPSED  COMMAND
32777   0.0   0.4  09:17    node /opt/homebrew/bin/openclaw doctor --fix
32778   1.1   4.8  09:17    openclaw
```

The managed Gateway had already been stopped at:

```text
06:49:37.575
Stopped the managed Gateway for Doctor repair.
```

More than nine minutes later, Doctor was still active.

## The large database integrity check itself is fast

For the 715 MiB main agent database:

```text
agentId: main
path: ~/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
elapsedMs: 2861
```

Phase breakdown:

```text
open:            0 ms
validation:    690 ms
configuration:   5 ms
schema:          10 ms
registration: 2156 ms
```

The actual integrity gate took only:

```text
integrityGateMs: 677
integrityGateOutcome: healthy
```

including:

```text
integrity_check:
  tableCount: 75
  elapsedMs: 537

quick_check:
  tableCount: 1
  elapsedMs: 124
```

Largest individual integrity checks included:

```text
transcript_events                  quick_check       124 ms
memory_embedding_cache            integrity_check   118 ms
memory_index_chunks_fts           integrity_check   106 ms
transcript_event_identities       integrity_check   100 ms
session_transcript_fts            integrity_check    69 ms
session_transcript_active_events  integrity_check    53 ms
```

So the ~715 MiB database itself is not spending minutes in SQLite integrity validation.

## Small databases show similar fixed registration overhead

The much smaller agents exhibit approximately the same ~2.15 s registration cost:

### 15 MiB agent

```text
agentId: runpod-qwen-a40
elapsedMs: 2190

validation:     21 ms
configuration:   4 ms
schema:          10 ms
registration: 2155 ms
integrityGateMs: 9 ms
```

### <1 MiB agent

```text
agentId: openclaw
elapsedMs: 2192

validation:      8 ms
configuration:   4 ms
schema:           7 ms
registration: 2173 ms
integrityGateMs: 1 ms
```

This suggests a significant fixed/serial registration cost independent of database size.

## Long gaps occur after normal agent DB opening

After the agent DB opens complete, Doctor continues performing state-database maintenance operations.

Examples:

```text
operation=agent.database.maintenance.lease
elapsedMs=1769
```

and repeated:

```text
operation=agent.database.maintenance.admission
elapsedMs=3927

operation=agent.database.maintenance.admission
elapsedMs=3905

operation=agent.database.maintenance.admission
elapsedMs=3914
```

Other slow transactions include:

```text
operation=state.write
elapsedMs=2221
```

```text
operation=plugins.lifecycle.lease
elapsedMs=1765
```

```text
operation=plugins.lifecycle.lease
elapsedMs=1769
```

```text
operation=state.plugin-migration-deferral
elapsedMs=1778
```

All of these are logged as:

```text
slow SQLite transaction hold
```

## Repeated SQLite revision/content-version worker activity

While Doctor is still running, short-lived child processes are observed such as:

```text
node .../dist/infra/sqlite-source-revision.worker.js \
  --openclaw-sqlite-readonly-child \
  content-version \
  ~/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite
```

Example:

```text
40449 32778 00:00 node ... sqlite-source-revision.worker.js \
  --openclaw-sqlite-readonly-child content-version \
  /Users/.../.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite
```

The worker is short-lived, but similar workers appear repeatedly during the long-running Doctor process.

This suggests that source/content revision work may be repeatedly serialized or recomputed instead of cached/reused during a single Doctor run.

## Important distinction: database health is good

This does not currently look like database corruption.

The main agent DB reports:

```text
integrityGateOutcome: healthy
```

and the table-level checks complete quickly.

There is also no observed `SQLITE_BUSY` failure in this run.

The issue is primarily excessive wall-clock time / repeated serialized maintenance work.

## Expected behavior

For healthy databases, `doctor --fix` should avoid repeatedly performing expensive revision, registration, or maintenance work when the same database has already been validated during the current Doctor run.

A 715 MiB agent DB whose integrity check completes in ~0.7 seconds should not cause Doctor to keep the Gateway offline for 9+ minutes.

Ideally:

- integrity/schema checks should be performed once per DB per Doctor run;
- source/content revision should be cached where safe;
- independent agent DB inspections could run concurrently;
- repeated maintenance admission/lease operations should be coalesced where possible;
- Doctor should report progress for long database maintenance phases;
- Gateway downtime should be minimized by doing read-only/preparation work before stopping the Gateway where possible.

## Actual behavior

Doctor:

1. starts normally;
2. stops the managed Gateway;
3. opens and validates all agent databases successfully;
4. reports healthy integrity checks;
5. continues for many additional minutes with low CPU utilization;
6. repeatedly performs state maintenance / lease / revision work;
7. provides little indication of why the command is still running.

At the time of inspection:

```text
doctor --fix elapsed: >9 minutes
CPU: ~0–1%
main agent DB: 715 MiB
main DB integrity gate: 677 ms
Gateway: stopped for Doctor repair
```

## Impact

This creates several practical problems:

- `doctor --fix` appears hung even though it is still working.
- Gateway downtime can extend to many minutes.
- Repair after an update becomes operationally expensive.
- Larger long-lived installations are disproportionately affected.
- Users may interrupt Doctor because there is no visible progress.
- Update flows that invoke Doctor inherit this latency.

## Possible areas to investigate

1. Repeated `sqlite-source-revision.worker.js content-version` invocations.
2. Whether database content-version/source-revision is recomputed multiple times in one Doctor run.
3. Serial execution of agent database inspection and registration.
4. The approximately fixed ~2.15 s `registration` cost for every agent DB.
5. Repeated `agent.database.maintenance.admission` transactions taking ~3.9 s each.
6. Repeated maintenance/plugin leases against `state/openclaw.sqlite`.
7. Whether read-only analysis can occur before the Gateway is stopped.
8. Whether results from integrity/schema/content-revision checks can be reused across Doctor phases.
9. Whether independent DB operations could safely run in parallel.
10. Adding phase/progress logging for operations expected to exceed several seconds.

## Related issues

Possibly related, but not identical:

- #164948 — `doctor --fix` self-deadlocks on `state/openclaw.sqlite` due to its own read connection / `SQLITE_BUSY`.
  - This report differs because no `SQLITE_BUSY` failure is observed; Doctor continues running.
- #162737 — candidate migration rehearsal hits a flat 300 s cap with a large agent DB.
- #160386 — large session stores cause severe SQLite I/O pressure and slow startup/runtime behavior.

This issue is specifically about **healthy large agent databases causing extremely long `doctor --fix` wall-clock time even though the measured integrity checks themselves complete quickly**.

## Additional evidence available

Full Doctor logs and additional timing samples can be provided if useful.

issue_title: [Bug] PTY sanitizer corrupts valid UTF-8 across read boundaries
issue_description:
### Self Checks

- [x] I have read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Language Policy](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/issues/1542).
- [x] This is only for bug report, if you would like to ask a question, please head to [Discussions](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/discussions/categories/general).
- [x] I have searched for existing issues [search for existing issues](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/issues), including closed ones.
- [x] I confirm that I am using English to submit this report, otherwise it will be closed.
- [x] 【中文用户 & Non English User】请使用英语提交，否则会被关闭 ：）
- [x] Please do not modify this template :) and fill in all the required fields.

### Dify version

Source `main` at `ca27376211cea79670614ffcbb9805d827cd17f3`, `dify-agent-runtime` component. Reproduced with Go 1.26.2 on Linux.

### Cloud or Self Hosted

Self Hosted (Source).

This is a component-level reproduction against the actual Go source package; the Dify API/Web stack, tmux, and Docker were not started.

### Steps to reproduce

The PTY sanitizer consumes ordinary byte chunks through `io.Reader`. A valid UTF-8 rune can span two reads. `PtySanitizer.Feed` currently decodes each chunk immediately without preserving an incomplete UTF-8 suffix.

1. Check out the commit above.
2. Add this temporary regression test as `dify-agent-runtime/internal/sanitize/utf8_read_boundary_repro_test.go`:

```go
package sanitize

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"testing"
)

type utf8BoundaryReader struct {
	data      []byte
	chunkSize int
}

func (r *utf8BoundaryReader) Read(p []byte) (int, error) {
	if len(r.data) == 0 {
		return 0, io.EOF
	}
	n := min(len(p), r.chunkSize, len(r.data))
	copy(p, r.data[:n])
	r.data = r.data[n:]
	return n, nil
}

func TestUTF8ReadBoundaries(t *testing.T) {
	const input = "Hello, 世界 🌍\n"
	for _, chunkSize := range []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, len(input)} {
		t.Run(fmt.Sprintf("chunk_%d", chunkSize), func(t *testing.T) {
			reader := &utf8BoundaryReader{data: []byte(input), chunkSize: chunkSize}
			var output bytes.Buffer
			if err := Run("", reader, &output); err != nil {
				t.Fatal(err)
			}
			if got := output.String(); got != input {
				t.Errorf("got %q; want %q", got, input)
			}
		})
	}
}
```

3. Run from `dify-agent-runtime`:

```bash
go test ./internal/sanitize -mod=readonly -count=1 -v
```

The reader limits each read to a small number of bytes. It only changes the read boundaries; the input bytes remain the same valid UTF-8 text. The full-input case is a control.

Relevant source:
- [Chunk decoding in Feed](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/blob/ca27376211cea79670614ffcbb9805d827cd17f3/dify-agent-runtime/internal/sanitize/sanitize.go#L38-L53)
- [Run passes ordinary read chunks into Feed](https://github.com/langgenius/dify/blob/ca27376211cea79670614ffcbb9805d827cd17f3/dify-agent-runtime/internal/sanitize/sanitize.go#L162-L187)

### ✔️ Expected Behavior

All chunk sizes produce exactly `Hello, 世界 🌍\n`. Sanitized text should be independent of read boundaries when the complete input is valid UTF-8.

Existing ANSI removal, carriage-return handling, and EOF behavior should remain compatible.

### ❌ Actual Behavior

The existing seven sanitizer tests pass. In the added test, chunk sizes 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 fail; the 19-byte full-input control passes.

Representative output:

```text
=== RUN   TestUTF8ReadBoundaries/chunk_1
    utf8_read_boundary_repro_test.go:35: got "Hello, ������ ����\n"; want "Hello, 世界 🌍\n"
=== RUN   TestUTF8ReadBoundaries/chunk_5
    utf8_read_boundary_repro_test.go:35: got "Hello, 世界 ����\n"; want "Hello, 世界 🌍\n"
    --- PASS: TestUTF8ReadBoundaries/chunk_19 (0.00s)
```

A read ending partway through a valid rune is treated as invalid bytes and replaced with U+FFFD, so the original characters cannot be recovered from the next chunk. This affects the PTY text observation consumed by the Agent.

I would like to contribute a focused fix with regression coverage for split UTF-8 runes, while preserving existing sanitizer behavior.

issue_title: Compaction rewrites live prompt prefix, preventing KV cache reuse on local OpenAI-compatible backends
issue_description:
﻿## Summary

OpenClaw compaction currently rebuilds the summarization request with a different system/user prompt instead of preserving the final prompt prefix used by the live foreground turn.

For local OpenAI-compatible backends that keep KV/prefix cache (llama.cpp, vLLM APC, etc.), this makes compaction start from token 0 with `cached_tokens=0`, even when the entire live conversation prefix is already resident in KV cache.

This is related to, but distinct from, #110564. That issue focuses on avoiding forced map-reduce when a single pass fits. The problem here is that even a single-pass compaction request can still miss the cache if OpenClaw rewrites the live prompt prefix.

## Environment

- OpenClaw: `2026.9.2 (3928bad)`
- Provider: self-hosted OpenAI-compatible `local-llm`
- Backend: llama.cpp behind llama-swap
- Model: Ornith 1.5 35B A3B, 262144-token context
- Endpoint: `/v1/chat/completions`
- Tools in live request: 52

## Observed behavior before patch

A normal foreground request and the immediately following compaction request used the same model and the same 52 tool definitions, but the message prefix differed.

Example capture:

```text
Foreground request:
  input_tokens: 31,543
  cached_tokens: 0
  messages: [system, user]
  tools: 52
  tool_choice: auto

Compaction request:
  input_tokens: 31,585
  cached_tokens: 0
  messages: [system, user, assistant, user]
  tools: 52
  tool_choice: none
```

The tool schema hash was identical, but the first two message hashes differed.

The live foreground system prompt contained runtime shaping such as:

```text
<!-- openclaw:attempt:STABLE -->
...
```

and other final runtime additions (surface/session/channel/capability context). The compaction path rebuilt its own prompt without exactly preserving those final bytes. The user message also differed because normal foreground shaping had already added the runtime timestamp, while the compaction reconstruction used the pre-shaped message.

Result: llama.cpp could not reuse the resident KV prefix and reported `cached_tokens=0`.

On a real 205,015-token session, staged compaction generated several cold summarization calls (for example ~31K, 16K, 33K, 15K prompt chunks), each with no useful foreground-prefix reuse.

## Minimal A/B proof outside OpenClaw

Using the exact same ~48K-token prefix twice against the same llama.cpp backend:

1. First request: full prefix, `cached_tokens=0`.
2. Second request: keep the prefix byte-for-byte identical and only append a final compaction instruction.

Result:

```text
First request:
  input_tokens: 48,023
  cached_tokens: 0
  duration: ~12.1 s

Second request:
  cached_tokens: 48,019
  new input tokens: 34
  duration: ~2.38 s
```

So the backend itself is fully capable of reusing the live KV for compaction. The cache miss comes from request shaping in OpenClaw.

## Verified local patch

I tested a transport-level prototype that keeps a transient per-session snapshot of the **final payload actually sent to the model** after OpenClaw's normal request shaping.

For a compaction request marked as cache-aware, the transport reuses the stored `messages + tools` prefix and appends only the compaction-specific suffix. Compaction keeps its own output settings (`tool_choice=none`, compaction max tokens, normal compaction reasoning settings).

The snapshot is in-memory only; if there is no compatible snapshot, normal compaction behavior remains the fallback.

### Production verification

Fresh session after gateway restart:

```text
Foreground warm request:
  input_tokens: 31,530
  cached_tokens: 0

Immediate compaction:
  cached_tokens: 31,613
  new input tokens: 538
  duration: ~8.1 s
```

The foreground and compaction captures were checked directly:

```text
first-two-messages SHA256: MATCH
52-tool payload SHA256:    MATCH
```

The compaction request still used its normal compaction settings:

```text
reasoning_effort: low
max_tokens: 16000
tool_choice: none
```

After compaction, a normal follow-up request in the same session correctly recalled an identifier from the pre-compaction turn and itself reported:

```text
cacheRead: 31,460
new input: 597
```

So the cache-aware path preserved both session continuity and subsequent prefix reuse.

## Suggested upstream design

The important part is not the exact prototype implementation, but the invariant:

> A compaction request should preserve the already-sent foreground prompt prefix byte-for-byte whenever possible, and add the summarization instruction as a suffix.

Possible implementation approaches:

1. Capture the final shaped foreground payload per session at the transport boundary and reuse that prefix for compaction.
2. Or expose/reuse the exact post-shaping system/messages representation from the foreground runner instead of reconstructing it in the compaction runner.
3. Keep the current staged/chunked compaction as a fallback when a single cache-aware request would exceed the context window or when no compatible live-prefix snapshot exists.

A transport-boundary snapshot was the most reliable prototype in my testing because it automatically includes timestamps, `STABLE/DYNAMIC` markers, surface/channel context, tool ordering, and future prompt-shaping changes without duplicating those rules in the compaction code.

## Why this matters

For local long-context models, prefill is often the dominant cost of compaction. Re-reading tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens that are already in KV cache is unnecessary work. Preserving the live prefix turns compaction from another cold long-context prefill into mostly summary generation plus a small suffix prefill.

This should also complement #110564: single-pass compaction gives the largest benefit when the single pass is constructed as a true extension of the live cached prefix rather than as a separately reconstructed summarization prompt.

---

Behavior and timings above were captured on a real deployment; the patch was validated end-to-end with llama-swap/llama.cpp activity captures.

issue_title: Released 2026.9.2 install updating to main passes the core switch, then Doctor fails on agent schema 19→20 and the service is left stopped
issue_description:
## What happens

Reproduced in a container with a real released 2026.9.2 install (populated state, stock workspace) updating with the released 9.2 updater to current main:

- The core switch succeeds (Git HEAD becomes the main commit).
- The post-switch Doctor then refuses the agent schema migration 19→20 (`doctor-failed`); recovery reports `state-migration-started`.
- The service is left **inactive**; HTTP health is refused.

The dev-install variant of the same update refuses *before* activation (the schema guard sees the update in progress and blocks pending agent migrations first), so the old service keeps running. The released-install path only discovers the refusal after the switch, when the old service is already gone.

## Expected

The updater treats a failed post-switch Doctor the way it treats a pre-activation refusal: keep or restore the previous service and report the refusal, instead of leaving the host without a Gateway. (Whether the 19→20 migration should be admitted during an update is the separate question tracked in #144005; this report is about the updater's failure handling.)

## Where

Update finalization / failure handling in the update CLI after the core switch (`src/cli/update-cli`), with the schema guard at `src/commands/doctor-update-schema-guard.ts` as the refusal source. Related tracker: #145252; companion report: #142681.

AI-assisted reproduction; exact command matrix retained by the maintainer.

issue_title: [BUG] MLX nvfp4: admitted request stalls in prefill at processed=total-1 with zero tokens for minutes under sustained single-slot load; only runner SIGTERM recovers
issue_description:
## Summary

Under sustained back-to-back load through a single slot (`OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1`), an admitted request on an MLX nvfp4 model intermittently stops making any progress — no further prompt-processing progress marks, no generated tokens — for minutes, while the `mlx` runner subprocess keeps spinning at 71–79% CPU. Client timeouts eventually cancel the request. The stall is runner-state-dependent, not content-dependent: the **same 7,213-token request froze twice and then completed in 12.6 s on the third attempt** (full log trace below).

A sharp fingerprint: in the two stalled attempts, prefill progress stopped at **`processed = total − 1`** tokens (5434/5435, then 3/4) and never transitioned to generation.

## Environment

- ollama 0.34.0 (macOS app)
- `MLX engine initialized "MLX version"=0.32.2-27-g37c26e5 device=gpu` (mlx_metal_v4, xgrammar v0.2.5)
- macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Apple M4 Max, 128 GiB RAM
- Model: `qwen3.5:4b-nvfp4` (`Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, 923 tensors)
- Server env (relevant): `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1`, `OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE=512`, `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=262144`, `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=5m0s`, `OLLAMA_DEBUG=INFO`
- A second model (`nomic-embed-text` served via llama-server) runs on the same ollama server for embeddings — it stayed fully healthy through every stall (see below)

## Symptom

Workload: a document-extraction pipeline drives the single slot continuously for ~60–100 min windows with 2–9K-token prompts (~4 concurrent client tasks queueing into the one slot). During these windows, intermittently (at least once per window in our observations):

1. A request is admitted (prefix-cache hit logged).
2. Prefill progress marks appear normally for the first ~1.5 s, then stop at `processed = total − 1`.
3. No further progress marks and no tokens for minutes, until the client deadline cancels.
4. The runner subprocess stays at 71–79% CPU throughout (observed via `ps` during stalls).
5. Requests admitted after the stall also hang; only SIGTERM of the runner subprocess recovers (see Recovery).

Healthy request latencies escalate in the minutes before each stall: 45 s → 1m08 → 1m15 → 1m26 → 1m42.

## Key evidence — same prompt, three attempts (2026-09-17, log timestamps +08:00 local)

**Attempt 1 — stalls in prefill at 5434/5435, then silent for 4m55s:**

```
11:31:38.298  prefix_cache.go:125  msg="cache hit" total=7213 matched=1781 cached=1778 left=5435
11:31:39.644  pipeline.go:223       msg="Prompt processing progress" processed=2048 total=5435
11:31:40.996  pipeline.go:223       msg="Prompt processing progress" processed=4096 total=5435
11:31:41.892  pipeline.go:223       msg="Prompt processing progress" processed=5434 total=5435
              <4 min 55 s of silence — no further marks, no tokens; runner at 71-79% CPU>
[GIN] 11:36:36 | 500 | 5m0s | POST "/api/chat"
11:36:36.645  server.go:235  ServeHTTP POST /v1/completions took=5m0.0236905s status="200 OK"

issue_title: [Bug]: Plugin source capture rewrites ~1.1–1.4 GB per CLI command and ~6.5 GB per Gateway start (no reuse, bundled native binaries): severe SSD wear
issue_description:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Since 2026.9.5, every process that loads the plugin runtime byte-copies and SHA-256-hashes every file of every externally installed plugin into a fresh capture directory, including the large native executables bundled with the official `codex` and `acpx` plugins. Nothing is reused across processes or deduplicated within one Gateway, so a single CLI command writes ~1.1–1.4 GB and a single Gateway start ~6.5 GB. With a usage monitor that runs `openclaw status --usage --json` every 5 minutes, this alone amounts to ~350–400 GB/day of SSD writes.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install OpenClaw 2026.9.6 (npm global) with the official external plugins `@openclaw/codex`, `@openclaw/acpx`, `@openclaw/discord`, `@openclaw/whatsapp` and `@openclaw/perplexity-plugin` enabled.
2. Record the disk's written sectors (`/sys/block/<device>/stat`, field 7).
3. Run `openclaw doctor --lint` (or `openclaw status --usage --json`) and watch `<stateDir>/tmp/plugin-captures/` while it runs.
4. Restart the Gateway and measure `<stateDir>/tmp/plugin-captures/<instance>/` once it is ready.
5. Compare the written sectors again.

### Expected behavior

Before 2026.9.5, plugins loaded from their install directory. An installed, unchanged plugin should not be recopied on every process start. At most one verified snapshot per plugin digest should exist and be reused by later processes, and certainly within one Gateway. Large immutable native executables should not be byte-copied at all.

### Actual behavior

- One `openclaw doctor --lint` run was measured at a peak of 4 `openclaw-plugin-build-*` captures totalling 1,127 MB, deleted at exit, and the disk recorded 1,393 MB written during the run. `openclaw status --usage --json` captures the same plugins. These commands take 52 s and 44 s, most of it copying and hashing.
- The largest copied files are bundled native binaries that never change:
  - `codex` plugin (372 MB per copy): `@openai/codex-linux-x64/.../bin/codex` (~269 MB) and `codex-code-mode-host` (~69 MB).
  - `acpx` plugin (618 MB per copy): a second Codex binary (~259 MB) plus `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk-linux-x64/claude` (~215 MB).
- One Gateway start produced one capture instance of **6.5 GB / ~92,000 files**. It held 4 separate copies of `acpx` (618 MB each), 3 of `codex` (372 MB each), 2 of `discord`, 3 of `whatsapp`, and a 2.6 GB `openclaw-model-catalog-*` capture.
- The capture loop reads each file, hashes it and writes a new copy (`writeFileSync`). It does not use hardlinks, reflinks or content-addressed reuse.
- Side effect (see #157351): each such process also leaves ~2,800 orphaned Node compile-cache files, because the capture paths are random. On one host this exhausted a 4.2M-inode `/tmp` in 5.6 days, and every `mktemp` on the machine then failed.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.6 (eb377ac)

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64 (Linux 6.8)

### Install method

npm global install, Gateway as a systemd user service, Node 26.8.2

### Model

Not model-specific: this happens during plugin loading, before any model request.

### Provider / routing chain

N/A (plugin runtime loading)

### Impact and severity

**Severe SSD wear and host-wide resource exhaustion.**

- **SSD writes:** a usage monitor running `openclaw status --usage --json` every 5 minutes (288 runs/day × ~1.1–1.4 GB) writes ~350–400 GB/day from this alone. The data SSD recorded ~5.1 TB written in 5.8 days of uptime (~880 GB/day in total, other workloads included). At that rate, a consumer SSD rated 600 TBW is used up in about 4 years from this cause alone; at the measured total, in about 2 years.
- **Any scheduled or scripted CLI use multiplies it:** health checks, `doctor --lint`, monitoring, cron jobs. Each Gateway start costs several GB more.
- **CPU and latency:** plugin-loading commands take 44–52 s.
- **Inode exhaustion:** the orphaned compile-cache entries (#157351) filled `/tmp`, which breaks unrelated software on the host.

Related:
- #157351: CLI recapture; closed without fixing the recapture.
- #157528: bounds the compile cache and explicitly leaves cross-process capture reuse out of scope.
- #157568: the Gateway regrows 7.5 GB of captures.
- #156191: catalog generation churn.

### Additional information

Suggested fixes:
1. A content-addressed capture store keyed by the package digest, shared across processes and reused within a process.
2. Do not byte-copy large immutable native executables. Verify them by digest and reference them in place, or use hardlinks/reflinks where the filesystem allows.
3. Let read-only CLI commands such as `status --usage` avoid loading the full plugin runtime. The Gateway's `usage.status` RPC answers the same query in ~2 s and creates no captures.

Workarounds that helped:
- For monitoring, use `openclaw gateway call usage.status --json` instead of `openclaw status --usage --json`.
- Run scheduled plugin-loading commands with `NODE_DISABLE_COMPILE_CACHE=1`. This prevents the orphaned compile-cache files, with no measurable slowdown (`doctor --lint` took 52 s either way).
- Put `<stateDir>/tmp/plugin-captures` on tmpfs to keep the copies off the SSD. RAM use equals the live capture size.

issue_title: Control UI: stale client state — duplicated assistant bubbles (stream vs final) and deleted sessions persisting in Home dock until hard refresh
issue_description:
## Summary

The Control UI (web client) fails to reconcile live-pushed state against server truth in two related ways. Both persist indefinitely — including across a full Gateway restart — and both clear instantly on a hard refresh (F5), so the server state is correct and the defect is client-side.

**Environment:** OpenClaw 2026.9.3 (1391f7c), Linux (WSL2), Control UI in Firefox, webchat channel, `claude-cli` agent runtime.

## Symptom 1: assistant replies rendered twice in webchat

Every assistant reply in an active webchat conversation shows as two bubbles. The two copies differ slightly in rendering (which presumably defeats the identical-bubble collapse described in `docs/web/control-ui/chat.md`), consistent with one bubble built from the live stream and a second from the final committed message, without deduplication between them.

Server-side checks all show exactly one copy:

- The CLI turn log shows a single model turn per reply (unique output hash per turn).
- `transcript_events` in the agent sqlite store contains exactly one copy of each reply (verified by searching a distinctive reply phrase).
- `conversation_deliveries` shows no duplicate `message_hash` entries.
- After a hard refresh, the conversation history renders every reply exactly once.

## Symptom 2: deleted sessions keep showing in the Home dock

Eleven finished subagent sessions were archived and then deleted via the `sessions` tool (`action: "delete"`, each returning `deleted: true` with a `.zst` transcript archive). `sessions_list` confirmed they no longer exist. The Home dock continued showing them:

- after archiving,
- after deletion,
- and even after a full Gateway restart (new process, new pid).

A hard refresh of the tab removed them immediately.

## Expected

- Stream-rendered bubbles should be replaced by (or deduplicated against) the final committed message, even when the streamed text and final text differ slightly.
- Session archive/delete events should update connected clients, or the client should revalidate its session list against the server on reconnect (a Gateway restart forces a reconnect, and the stale entries still survived that).

## Notes

- Both issues reproduce reliably in the same client session; a single F5 clears both, which is what points at client-side state reconciliation rather than the Gateway.
- Happy to provide additional logs or run diagnostics against a dev build if useful.

issue_title: buzz: a session tombstoned by restart recovery silently fails every later mention in that room; CLI cannot delete/reset channel-scoped keys
issue_description:
## Summary

After a crash loop (#144911 on this install), `main-session-restart-recovery` tombstoned a Buzz group session that had been mid-turn. From then on **every mention to that agent in that room failed silently**: the only trace is one line per message in the JSON log, and nothing reaches the room, the dead-letter list, or the main gateway log. Other agents in the same room, whose sessions were idle during the crashes, kept answering normally, so from the operator's seat it looks like one bot ignoring people.

## Observed (2026.9.4, macOS, launchd)

```
08:10:05 [main-session-restart-recovery] tombstoned main-session restart recovery:
         agent:claude-code:buzz:group:buzz:<room> (blocked after 3 automatic attempts without a started runtime turn …)
08:10:06 sent restart recovery tombstone notice   ← one message in the room, once
…
17:44:58 [claude] Buzz message failed: Session "agent:claude-code:buzz:group:buzz:<room>" ended during restart recovery.
         Use /new or /reset to start a replacement session.
```

That failure line repeated **12 times** over five hours, three of them for the owner's direct questions, with the agent's other room sessions working fine throughout.

## What made it hard to remediate

- `openclaw sessions delete <key> --agent <id>` fails on Buzz keys: `Error: Buzz target must be a channel UUID` (the live-artifact cleanup tries to resolve the key as a delivery target).
- There is no `sessions reset` / `sessions new` CLI verb, though the error text tells the user to use `/new` or `/reset`.
- `sessions.delete` over `gateway call` works with `{agentId, key}` but rejects `dryRun`, so there is no preview.

`sessions.delete` via RPC returned `deleted: true`, archived the transcript, and the next inbound created a fresh session that answered normally.

## Suggestions

1. A tombstoned session should not silently fail subsequent inbound. Either auto-create the replacement session on the next inbound (the tombstone notice already told the user the transcript is safe), or surface each failure as a dead letter / a `[buzz/inbound]` line in the main log so a watcher can see it.
2. Make the CLI `sessions delete` path work for channel-scoped keys, or add the `reset` verb the error message promises.
3. Consider a `dryRun` on `sessions.delete`.

Related: #144911 (the crash loop that produced the tombstone), #144203 (other silent Buzz inbound loss on this install).

issue_title: MCP stdio server with a missing launcher binary (e.g. uvx not installed) fails silently as generic "Connection closed"
issue_description:
## Summary

When a plugin's `mcpServers` entry runs via `uvx` (or presumably any other external launcher binary) and that binary isn't installed on the host at all, the failure surfaces — if it surfaces anywhere — as a generic `MCP error -32000: Connection closed`, with nothing pointing at "the launcher binary doesn't exist." On a normal gateway boot, nothing surfaces at all: the MCP server is apparently started lazily/on-demand rather than at boot, so a missing `uvx` produces total silence until something actually tries to use the tool (or until `openclaw doctor --fix`'s health probe touches it).

This is a distinct issue from the two existing closed "Connection closed" reports — #122021 (non-JSON banner before JSON-RPC) and #144997 (`command` pointing at a directory) — which are different specific causes producing the same generic message. This one is the simplest and probably most common case: the command in `mcpServers.<name>.command` just isn't on `PATH` at all (`ENOENT` at spawn time).

## Repro

1. Install/enable any plugin whose manifest declares an `mcpServers` entry with `command: "uvx"` (matching the example in `docs/gateway/config-extensions.md`) on a host that has never installed `uv`/`uvx`.
2. Restart the gateway. No error appears anywhere (file logs at debug, `openclaw health --json`, `journalctl`) — the plugin's config/manifest loads fine, its MCP server is just never started.
3. Run `openclaw doctor --fix`. Its MCP health probe is what actually attempts to spawn the server, and reports:
   ```
   [bundle-mcp] failed to start server "<name>" (uvx <pkg> (cwd=...)): MCP error -32000: Connection closed
   ```
4. `which uvx` / `command -v uvx` on the host returns nothing — confirming the binary is simply absent, not a transport/JSON-RPC bug.

## Why this matters

- A user installing a `uvx`-based plugin from ClawHub gets no actionable signal that they need to install `uv` first — the Control UI shows "enabled," and only a proactive `openclaw doctor --fix` run (not something most users know to run after every plugin install) reveals the real cause, buried behind a generic JSON-RPC error code.
- This is likely to affect a meaningful share of ClawHub plugins: any Python-based MCP server wrapped via `uvx` (the pattern OpenClaw's own docs use as the canonical example) hits this exact failure mode on any host without `uv` preinstalled.

## Suggested direction

- At minimum, when a stdio MCP server's `command` resolves to nothing on `PATH` (a simple `ENOENT`/pre-flight `which`-style check), surface a specific, actionable error — "command `uvx` not found on PATH; install it: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/" — instead of the generic `-32000: Connection closed`.
- Consider whether plugin install (`openclaw plugins install`) should proactively check `mcpServers.*.command` binaries at install time and warn immediately, rather than only at first use or during an explicit `doctor --fix` run.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.9.4, systemd user service, Raspberry Pi (aarch64), Node v24
- Plugin used to reproduce: a ClawHub-installed plugin with `mcpServers.<name> = {command: "uvx", args: ["<pypi-package>"]}` and zero other manifest surfaces

session: two server processes sharing one opencode.db allocate session_message.seq independently - UNIQUE(seq) collisions fail sessions
issue_description:
### Description

When two opencode server processes share a single `opencode.db` (a long-lived `opencode serve --service` instance plus a TUI-embedded server from `opencode -c`), both allocate `session_message.seq` from independent in-memory counters. The second server's counter starts from a stale/near-empty view of the session, and as it advances it collides with rows already persisted by the first server: every colliding insert fails with `UNIQUE constraint failed: session_message.session_id, session_message.seq`, surfacing as "Session failed" in the UI and permanently breaking the session on that server.

### OpenCode version

2.0.22 (channel latest); the same topology exists fleet-side on 1.18.34.

### Operating System

Linux x64

### Plugins

None installable; MCP servers only (via config).

### Steps to reproduce

1. `opencode serve --service` on a data dir (server B, fresh TUI clients attach here)
2. Run `opencode -c` (TUI with embedded server, no TCP listener) on the SAME data dir
3. Continue working the same session from both processes
4. Server B's in-memory seq counter advances into seqs already persisted by server A -> `UNIQUE constraint failed: session_message.session_id, session_message.seq`, turns fail

### Screenshot and/or share link

Log + DB evidence inline below (no share link available).

## Observed failure

```
ERROR "Failed to drain Session"
  cause: EffectDrizzleQueryError: Failed query: insert into "session_message" (...) values (?, ...)
  [cause]: SQLiteError: UNIQUE constraint failed: session_message.session_id, session_message.seq
    at SessionRunner.publishLLMEvent -> SessionStep.attempt -> SessionRunner.runStep -> SessionRunner.drain
```

5 occurrences on one day, all against a single long-running session.

## Evidence (from the live DB after the incident)

Two interleaved write streams into the same `session_id`, each with its own counter:

- Stream A (original server): counter intact across a day - wrote seqs 385-736 between 06:18-06:45 UTC.
- Stream B (second server): initialized from a near-empty view of the session - first write landed on seq 2 at 06:51 UTC, then advanced ~19 seqs per assistant turn (2, 17, 32, 51, 70, 89, 113 ... 710 by 12:52 UTC).
- Stream B's inserts succeed only where Stream A left gaps (its ephemeral/unpersisted seqs) and fail exactly where Stream A persisted rows:
  - seq 108: occupied since the previous day -> fail
  - seq 585 (+cascade 586): occupied 48 min earlier -> fail
  - seq 684: occupied 6 h earlier -> fail
  - seq 709: occupied 6 h earlier -> fail (the "Session failed" the user saw)
- Follow-up `idle` messages (+1 seq) inserted fine immediately after each failure (109, 685, 710 were free), which is why the session half-works and the failure looks intermittent.

Ruled out: disk space, `SQLITE_BUSY`, FK violations (`session_v2` row exists), DB corruption (`quick_check` ok).

## Root cause

`session_message.seq` is allocated per-process from in-memory runner state, while the database is shared. Nothing prevents two server processes from serving the same data directory and the same session, and nothing reconciles their counters. The first server to touch the session wins; the second replays an overlapping seq space and aborts turns on collisions. TUI restarts make this easy to hit: the old server keeps running while a new one spawns (both hold the DB).

## Suggested directions

1. Allocate `seq` at insert time from the database (`SELECT max(seq)+1 ...` inside the write transaction, or an AUTOINCREMENT-style per-session counter table) instead of from in-memory runner state.
2. On `UniqueViolation` for `(session_id, seq)`, re-read the current max seq and retry the insert once instead of failing the whole session run.
3. Guard the data directory against a second live server (lock/heartbeat row), or make a later server adopt the session state (re-read max seq at session load).

## Related

- #52395 - same UNIQUE constraint on seq, but triggered by continuing a V1-created session (migration path), not by dual live servers.

issue_title: JSONC error caret drifts with multi-digit line numbers
issue_description:
### Description

JSONC parse errors render the caret with a fixed horizontal offset. The source prefix includes the line number, so its width grows at lines 10, 100, and so on, while the caret padding does not.

For example, the caret moves one additional column left when the same invalid token is moved from line 1 to line 10. It should remain directly below the reported character regardless of the line-number width.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Put an invalid token in `opencode.jsonc` on line 10 or later.
2. Start OpenCode or otherwise load the config.
3. Compare the printed `^` position with the invalid character in the displayed source line.

The drift increases at each line-number digit boundary.

Any

issue_title: How to wait for a browser re-render?  Vue.nextTick doesn't seem to cover it, and setTimeout(..., 0) is not good enough.
issue_description:
### What problem does this feature solve? Example in a fiddle: https://jsfiddle.net/szal/eywraw8t/500316/ - when I click Load, I never see the "Loading..." indicator. When I have a Vue component in a .vue file with a data member isLoading: false, and a template:
Loading...
And a method: loadIt() { this.isLoading = true this.$nextTick(() => { console.log(this.$refs.hey) // ...other synchronous work here that causes other DOM changes this.isLoading = false }) } ("Loading" here refers to loading from the in-memory store, not an AJAX request. I want to do this so that I can show a simple "loading" indicator instantly while the DOM changes that might take 0.2-0.5 second or so are occurring.) I thought that the $nextTick function would allow both the virtual and actual DOM to update. The console log reads that the item was "shown" (removing the display: none style). However, in both Chrome and Firefox, I never see the "Loading..." indicator; the short delay happens, and the other DOM changes happen without the Loading indicator being shown. If I use setTimeout instead of $nextTick, I will see the loading indicator, but only when the other work is sufficiently slow. If there is a delay of a few tenths of a second, the loading indicator never shows. I'd like it to appear immediately on click so that I can present a snappy GUI. My unsatisfying solution: I have to wrap the work in a setTimeout(..., 25), per seebiscuit's findings here: https://github.com/vuejs/vuex/issues/1023#issuecomment-358456384 This seems to reveal that the documentation on Vue.nextTick at https://vuejs.org/v2/api/#Vue-nextTick is inaccurate: "Defer the callback to be executed after the next DOM update cycle. Use it immediately after you’ve changed some data to wait for the DOM update." This seems wrong; this is a good case where the user doesn't see the DOM update at all even though Vue.nextTick was used. Calling setTimeout(..., 25) doesn't seem very discoverable or intuitive for anyone. ### What does the proposed API look like? I'd propose either a change to Vue.nextTick to work better, or a parallel call just like Vue.nextTick, perhaps "nextRender" (maybe there's a better name?) that ensures that any DOM changes can get displayed to the user before its callback is invoked asynchronously. So then I could do something like: methods: { async selectThing() { this.thingIsLoading = true // this triggers a dead-simple v-show await this.$nextRender() // the new Vue API call; give browser a chance to paint the loading indicator const route = setQuery(this.$route, 'thingid', this.thingViewModel.thing.id) this.$router.push(route) // this triggers lots of reactivity that may take a big fraction of a second to rerender/paint this.thingIsLoading = false } } If others feel that instead an enhancement to the behavior of Vue.nextTick is in order, I'd prefer that. I'd also propose changing the documentation at https://vuejs.org/v2/api/#Vue-nextTick to be more accurate and perhaps explain this limitation and a workaround to future developers.

issue_title: awesome-go.com pins golang.org/x/net v0.38.0: duplicate-attribute parse/render anomaly tree defeats the "Sanitize HTML" goquery roundtrip (CVE-2026-27136 / GO-2026-5030)
issue_description: # awesome-go.com pins golang.org/x/net v0.38.0: duplicate-attribute parse/render anomaly tree defeats the "Sanitize HTML" goquery roundtrip (CVE-2026-27136 / GO-2026-5030) Last saved at 2026-09-08 ## Asset avelino/awesome-go — the static site generator that builds awesome-go.com (SOURCE_CODE) and its pinned dependency **golang.org/x/net v0.38.0** (`go.mod:17`, pulled in via goquery v1.8.1 → cascadia). Affected scenario: the two goquery parse-then-serialize roundtrips the generator performs on rendered template output (`main.go:223-237`, whose source comment is literally labeled "Sanitize HTML"; `main.go:753-761`). Affected dependency version: `golang.org/x/net < 0.55.0` (the project's pin of v0.38.0 falls in range). Audit baseline: main branch commit `2222bc3e8d6af0a969a37640909413bf259ef235` (2026-09-07). ## Weakness Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (Cross-site Scripting) (cwe-79) — a parse-tree anomaly faithfully serialized such that browser semantics diverge from the sanitized/normalized result (i.e., the advisory's "sanitize input HTML before rendering" scenario fails) ## Description > **Version declaration:** This report targets the **avelino/awesome-go main @ `2222bc3e8d6af0a969a37640909413bf259ef235`** repository tree together with **golang.org/x/net v0.38.0** (OSV pinned commit `7770ec48d03fec35e378665337b4faca93c38423`, fixed version 0.55.0); advisory **CVE-2026-27136 / GO-2026-5030**: "Invoking duplicate attributes can cause XSS in golang.org/x/net/html", "Parsing arbitrary HTML which is then rendered using Render can result in an unexpected HTML tree. This can be leveraged to execute XSS attacks in applications that attempt to sanitize input HTML before rendering." The findings are **code-level white-box confirmations** (both-versions source diff + dependency-level minimal repro + full-pipeline twin builds); no live-service requests were performed in this submission. ### Summary awesome-go's generator writes README-derived content through templates and then performs two goquery (i.e., `golang.org/x/net/html` underneath) **parse-then-serialize roundtrips** on the output before deployment — one of them carries the source comment "Sanitize HTML" (`main.go:221-222`). Under x/net v0.38.0, **duplicate attributes** — a parse error per the HTML5 spec — are all retained in the node and serialized verbatim, while a browser re-parses first-occurrence-wins (case-insensitively) and only honors the **first** attribute. Any sanitizer/normalizer assuming "later value overrides earlier" (e.g., the map-normalization pattern used by x/net's own `copyAttributes`, `parse.go:850-862`) or "survivors after dedup" mis-trusts the safe value while the dangerous first attribute wins in the browser. The project pins v0.38.0, so duplicate-attribute payloads embedded in README inline HTML (admitted by goldmark `WithUnsafe`, entity-decoded by goquery `.Text()`, unescaped by `text/template`) sail through the self-described sanitizing roundtrip into the deployed pages. ### Finding A: x/net v0.38.0 retains duplicate attributes; v0.55.0 fixes to first-value-only **Files (dependency side):** x/net/html `tokenizer.go` (v0.38.0 `readTag` appends every `z.pendingAttr` into `z.attr` with no dedup) vs v0.55.0 (adds `attrNames map[string]bool`, dedups by lowercased key, keeps only the first occurrence). Fix diff: `xnet-token-go-fix-diff.patch`. **Files (project side):** `main.go:221-237`, `main.go:739-770` ```go // main.go:221-237 — renderCategories: goquery roundtrip, source comment says "Sanitize HTML" // Sanitize HTML. This is not necessary, but allows to have content // of all html files in same style. { doc, err := goquery.NewDocumentFromReader(buf) ... html, err := doc.Html() // x/net/html Parse + Render roundtrip ... os.WriteFile(categoryIndexFilename, []byte(html), 0644) } ``` Segment-by-segment: `doc.Html()` follows the x/net/html Parse → Render path. The v0.38.0 parser's `addElement` (`parse.go:325-332`) carries `p.tok.Attr` into the node verbatim — the node holds **all** duplicate attributes; `html.Render` serializes **all of them**. The HTML5 spec requires the tokenizer to flag duplicate attribute names as a parse error and keep only the first (first-occurrence-wins, case-insensitive). The v0.38.0 roundtrip output therefore diverges **semantically** from what any browser produces by re-parsing — the roundtrip is neither idempotent nor normalizing. The attack input chain matches the established README pipeline: community PR edits README → entity-encoded inline HTML (admitted by goldmark `WithUnsafe`) → goquery `extractCategories` `.Text()` decodes entities → `text/template` writes unescaped → the roundtrip parses with v0.38.0 → the anomaly tree is faithfully serialized into the deployed `out/` pages → the browser executes the first dangerous attribute. ### Finding B: Dependency-level minimal repro — a "last-wins-map" sanitizer is bypassed **Files (evidence):** `dependency-level/main.go`, `dependency-level/output_v0380.txt`, `dependency-level/output_v0550.txt` v0.38.0 (verbatim from `output_v0380.txt`): ``` === Payload P1 === input: click parsed tree attrs (v parser): [{a@href javascript:alert(1)} {a@href https://benign.example/safe}] Render output: click browser re-parse (first-wins): [a@href=javascript:alert(1)] last-wins-map sanitizer: blocked=false, emits [{a@href https://benign.example/safe}] verdict: *** BYPASS: sanitizer last-wins saw benign value, browser honors DANGEROUS first attr *** ``` Segment-by-segment: the parse tree holds both `href`s; Render emits both; a first-wins browser executes `javascript:alert(1)`; a last-wins-map sanitizer sees the benign `https://benign.example/safe` and sets `blocked=false` — **the sanitizer and the browser see different trees**. The mixed-case `HREF` variant hits identically (P2). For ``, both event handlers enter the tree/serialization and the value kept by a map sanitizer diverges from the value the browser executes (smuggling differential, P3). Under fixed v0.55.0 (`output_v0550.txt`): only the first attribute survives into the tree, the roundtrip is idempotent, the sanitizer sees the true first value and blocks it — 3/3 payloads verdict = blocked, no bypass. ### Finding C: Full-pipeline twin builds — the anomaly tree lands in deployed pages and vanishes with the dependency upgrade **Files (evidence):** `poc_projectA_duphref_anchor.txt`, `poc_projectB_duponerror_img.txt`, `poc_category_duphref_anchor.txt`, the `fixed_*` counterparts, `poc-vs-fixed-site-diff.patch`, `summary.json` PoC README (`workdir/poc/README.cve27136.md`), two payloads: ```html dup-attr-a ``` - **Vulnerable build (go.mod identical to upstream, x/net v0.38.0):** both the project page and the category page (both roundtrips) serialize `` and `` — the anomaly tree is faithfully serialized into the generated pages (`summary.json`, 6/6 assertions pass). - **Fixed twin build (only x/net upgraded to 0.55.0 plus its companion modules; `diff` of the two go.mod files confirms no other change):** the same README yields only the first attribute `` / `` — duplicate attributes disappear entirely, pinning the root cause to the x/net version. - `poc-vs-fixed-site-diff.patch` provides a byte-level comparison of the two builds (the static-attribute ordering differences in the diff are new-serializer behavior, unrelated to this CVE's security semantics). ### Versions Verified | Version | Duplicate-attribute handling | Roundtrip output | Sanitizer semantics | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | golang.org/x/net v0.38.0 (project pin, `go.mod:17`) | ❌ All retained (`z.attr = append(...)`, no dedup) | ❌ All duplicates serialized | ❌ Roundtrip non-idempotent; diverges from browser first-wins | | golang.org/x/net v0.55.0 (fixed, verified in twin build) | ✅ First value only (`attrNames` dedup) | ✅ Idempotent | ✅ Sanitizer sees the same tree as the browser | Advisory affected range `golang.org/x/net < 0.55.0`; the project falls in range. No upgrade commit was found in the audited tree. --- ## Steps To Reproduce **Pre-conditions:** An attacker opens a README PR containing entity-encoded duplicate-attribute inline HTML and a maintainer merges it; CI (`tests.yaml`/`site-deploy.yaml` both run `go run .`) builds and deploys. Local reproduction (white-box logic path, no online services): **Step 1 — dependency-level minimal repro.** Use the archived `dependency-level/` module (`main.go` + `go.mod`, defaulting to x/net v0.38.0): `go run .` with the three payloads starting from `click`; then in a twin module run `go get golang.org/x/net@v0.55.0 && go run .` as the fixed control. Expected: under v0.38.0 the tree holds all duplicates, Render serializes them verbatim, first-wins browser semantics execute the first value while a last-wins-map sanitizer passes (`output_v0380.txt`: P1/P2 verdict BYPASS); under v0.55.0 only the first value survives and the sanitizer blocks (`output_v0550.txt`: 3/3 blocked). **Step 2 — full-pipeline reproduction.** Run the archived script `workdir/repro/reproduce_cve2026_27136.sh` (AWESOME_SKIP_FETCH=1, GOPROXY pinned to a mirror): it stages two source copies — poc (x/net v0.38.0) and fixed (only x/net upgraded to 0.55.0) — both with the README `workdir/poc/README.cve27136.md` (payload A `<a href="javascript:alert(27136)" href="https://benign.example/safe">dup-attr-a</a>` and payload B `<img src=x onerror="alert(1)" onerror="alert(2)">`), and runs `go run .` on each. **Step 3 — inspect generated pages (expected results).** Vulnerable build: `out/poc-dup-attr-category/poc-repo-dup-a-poc-owner-github/index.html` (project page) and `out/poc-dup-attr-category/index.html` (category page) both contain `` (`poc_projectA_duphref_anchor.txt`, `poc_category_duphref_anchor.txt`) and `` (`poc_projectB_duponerror_img.txt`). Fixed build: the same README yields only the first attribute (`fixed_*` files). Byte-level diff: `poc-vs-fixed-site-diff.patch`; assertion results: `summary.json` (6/6 pass). **Step 4 — browser-semantics cross-check.** Re-verify under HTML5 tokenizer rules: duplicate attributes are a parse error and the browser DOM keeps only the **first** occurrence (case-insensitive) — i.e., `javascript:alert(27136)` and `onerror="alert(1)"` take effect — diverging from the "all attributes coexist" form serialized into the generated page, confirming the roundtrip is non-normalizing. **Actual vs. expected results:** Actual — the self-described "Sanitize HTML" goquery roundtrip, under x/net v0.38.0, writes the spec-violating duplicate-attribute structure verbatim into deployed pages; the fixed twin build, on identical input, produces roundtrip output consistent with browser semantics. Expected (secure behavior) — the roundtrip should yield a normalized tree (first duplicate only) so the sanitization assumption holds. The single varying variable between the two builds is the x/net version (verified via `diff` of both go.mod files); the chain is closed at source level. --- ## Impact | Aspect | Detail | | --- | --- | | **Attack requirement** | One README PR with duplicate-attribute payloads merged by a maintainer (normal community flow); same attack channel as the README-injection findings, but the root cause lives in the dependency | | **Privilege boundary** | The attacker causes pages deployed to awesome-go.com to carry attribute structures whose browser semantics diverge from the normalized result; no server privileges involved | | **Confidentiality** | The browser honors the first dangerous attribute (click-executed `javascript:` href, dual-`onerror` smuggling): same-origin script execution can read and exfiltrate same-origin data | | **Integrity** | Bypasses the project's own "Sanitize HTML" roundtrip; any downstream relying on that roundtrip to disambiguate attributes (cache/rewrite/minify pipelines) receives a tree inconsistent with browser semantics | | **Availability** | No server-side impact | | **Severity** | Medium. Advisory CVSS 3.1 `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N`; in this project's context the attacker first needs a merged PR (`PR:L`), netting ≈ 5.0–5.4 | | **CVE eligibility** | The root-cause CVE already exists (CVE-2026-27136 / GO-2026-5030, affecting x/net < 0.55.0); no new CVE ID is needed. This report serves as affected-consumer evidence for urging the project to upgrade | | **Suggested submission channels** | ① GitHub Issue per SECURITY.md (https://github.com/avelino/awesome-go/issues/new, with the upgrade recommendation `golang.org/x/net ≥ 0.55.0`); ② maintainer email avelinorun@gmail.com; ③ VulDB (https://vuldb.com/?submit, login required, may reference the existing CVE); ④ MITRE CNA-LR (https://mitre.github.io/mitre-cve-roles/cve-id-request/, fallback, only if coordination is needed) | Additional notes: - **Suggested fix:** upgrade `go.mod:17` to `golang.org/x/net v0.55.0` or later (with companion upgrades of x/sys and x/text; the twin build verifies the behavioral difference). After the upgrade the "Sanitize HTML" roundtrip output is idempotent and consistent with browser semantics. Long term, migrate the template stack to `html/template` to remove reliance on roundtrip sanitization. - **Relation to the text/template injection:** independently valid — even if the template layer is later fixed to escape, as long as the dependency stays at v0.38.0 the "sanitizing" roundtrip still fails to normalize duplicate attributes (proven by the fixed twin build: with the dependency fixed, roundtrip output matches browser semantics).

issue_title: VueSSRServerPlugin produces a slow-to-parse JSON for large projects
issue_description:
### What problem does this feature solve?
Makes for a better development experience with vue SSR.

I was looking into why it takes 500ms to render an single-component page from the server in our fairly large application and found an interesting issue. Webpack creates ~40 bundles for us. Altogether, these weigh ~20MB. The way  `VueSSRServerPlugin` plugin works, as you know, is it combines all of these files into a single `vue-ssr-server-bundle.json` file. Reading that file in node is fast (5ms on average) for us, but after reading it we need to `JSON.parse` it before providing to `createBundleRenderer` and _that_ takes ~400ms.

Initially I was thinking of using webpack's `splitChunks`, to reduce the file-size (our router dynamically imports top-level pages, so each chunk could benefit from not having to bring in common component) but `VueSSRServerPlugin` does not support that (and throws the "Server-side bundle should have one single entry file" error).

### What does the proposed API look like?
I'm not exactly sure what to do here at this point as I just noticed this issue. I'm concerned that as the app grows, the json parse time will increase adding seconds to the load-time in development.

issue_title: Issues with v-model.number
issue_description:
### Version
2.5.8

### Reproduction link
[https://jsfiddle.net/50wL7mdz/79189/](https://jsfiddle.net/50wL7mdz/79189/)

### Steps to reproduce
Included in fiddle

### What is expected?
Input type='number' should  not clear values, accept stings formatted in different locales. v-model.number should not return string.

### What is actually happening?
Input value is cleared sometimes, v-model.number returns "" for "" and partially typed numbers.

---
This issue started with topic on forum https://forum.vuejs.org/t/extra-directive-for-number-inputs/22438, it was suggested to open an issue for that. Here is original post:

Hi!

I've found that `v-model.number` has limitations and requires some boilerplate in some cases. This is mostly because `input[type="number"]` returns `''` for partially input numbers (like `1.`). Here are some problems with it:

- App has no difference when input is either empty or invalid/partial.
- Bound attribute has to be of `[String, Number]` type.
- `''`, `undefined`, and `0` are falsy values. This leads to `val !== ''` checks in all places this attribute is used.

2nd and 3d issues can be solved with computed property, but it's hard to implement for nested ones and array of values.

I came to using separate field for casted values: 

```
<input
  type='number' 
  v-model='obj.val' 
  @input='$set(obj, "valCasted", _nOrNull($event.target.value))'
/>
```

I wanted to it implement with custom directive (like `v-model-number='obj.valCasted'`), but I see that `v-model` is handled differently by compiler. This way it can automatically use `$set` when property is not defined on object. But I have not found how this  can be implemented with custom directives.

 So here are questions :)  :

- Is there a better way to work with `input[type="number"]`?
If not:
- Can this be implemented with custom directives as convenient as `v-model` is?
- Should this be added to vue?

-----

After that post I've tried to implement custom component, it's included in fiddle, but it also has some issues.
I've also added different types of inputs to fiddle to check their behaviour and checked against different locales.

Thank you!
